utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. This is Wednesday. I greet the accused and the counsel, also the witness, and the representatives of the Prosecutor's office, and all the people who are helping us in and around the court. The Registrar has to give us a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. 2D has submitted its response to the Prosecution's objections to its documents tendered via Witness Davor Korac. This list shall be given Exhibit IC989. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Before I give the floor to the witness, please, speak slower than usual, because the interpreters have some problems. Thank you for all the efforts you may make to make things better.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Prosecutor, I greet you also, and have you floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President, each of Your Honours, and everyone around the courtroom this afternoon. And good afternoon to you, Dr. Bagaric.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: You told us on Monday that you were a doctor and that you were also a politician; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you can put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: All right. I want to ask you a few questions about politics, if I may, and I want to start with a meeting in Tomislavgrad in December of 1991. All right? And what I want to start by doing is just to make sure we've got the right Ivan Bagaric, because you told us about another document that you thought that there might have been somebody else with your name in Herceg-Bosna at the time. So if you'd start, please, by looking with me at the first document in the binder you've just been given, P00089. Binder 1, I'm so sorry. All the documents are in binder 1. What we have in binder 2 are the transcripts from Dr. Bagaric's testimony in another case. So if you would look with me, please, Doctor, at P00089, and you'll see that at page 1 that we're at a meeting of the 27th of December of 1991, chaired by Dr. Franjo Tudjman, but if you'd turn on to page 20, and it's actually a very few pages in because we've taken out the intervening pages that don't concern us today, if you turn just one, two, three, four, five pages, you should find a page that has at the top an excerpt from the minutes of the 2nd regular session of the Presidency of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On page 20, yes, if that is that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: All right. And what's happening here, as we're going to see, is that a colleague of yours called Mr. Kostroman is reading the minutes of a meeting that took place in Tomislavgrad on the 23rd of December, 1991, all right, and towards the foot of the page he has a list of names of people who took part in the discussion. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't. Just bear with me for a moment. Let me try and see what we're talking about. It's in Tomislav --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues]... which makes our interpreting quite hard.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can see it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... it's on the same page in the B/C/S/ as it is in English, and it's page 20, and we have a list of names there. The session was chaired by President Mate Boban. Can you see that? And then three lines up from the bottom, we have your name, or a name that is also yours, "Ivan Bagaric." Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: And is that you who was at a meeting in Tomislavgrad in December of 1991, Dr. Bagaric?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I attended a lot of meetings. I don't know which one is this. I would have to be given a moment to look at it. Maybe I can explain, and this will be a direct answer to your question, if you give me a minute to explain things.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Well, I can give you any time you'd like to explain things, but I want to just get clear whether it's you or not. Tomislavgrad, I think, is your hometown, is it not?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I believe that this is my name at the foot, because it says "Ivan Bagaric." However, I would have to look at the whole thing more closely in order to be able to properly recognise it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: I understand that, and we're going to look at some of the things that were said at that meeting. And if you're in any doubt about whether it's you or not, you've only to tell us. I want to be clear with you whether that Ivan Bagaric is you. All right? Some of the other names there, Dario Kordic, Ante Valenta, Ivan Sarac, who you told us, I think in answer to a question by Judge Mindua, had become the head of the Ministry of Health and was a friend of yours; yes?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would the counsel speak into the microphone. The counsel's microphone is covered by his binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: I'm very sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I don't understand your question. Are you asking me whether my name is Ivan Bagaric, indeed, or whether I was the one attending the meeting? It says here "Ivan Bagaric." This is probably me. However, until I have a closer look at the thing, I can't say that for a fact. It says "Ivan Bagaric" here. My name is Ivan Bagaric. Your Honours, I attended a lot of meeting, and this may well have been one of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: If I may try to assist. Mr. Bagaric, are you aware of any person in Herzegovina who had an interest in politics and would attend such meetings, and who happened to have the same name; or have you not heard of another Ivan Bagaric who would attend such a meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, of course I'm not the only Ivan Bagaric. There is lots of them. The name is very common, the family name is very common. However, judging by the other names, I would assume that this was indeed me. I've already said that, and that's why I'm saying that I don't understand the gentleman's question, because I already confirmed that this was probably me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Can we turn the page, then, please, and see what was being discussed here. Item 1: "The Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna congratulates the entire people on achieving our historical objective - the establishment and final international recognition of the Republic of Croatia." And you see that?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: And then in the next paragraph, congratulations to Dr. Tudjman?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see all of that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: And then in item 2: "The Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna has once again confirmed the will of the entire Croatian people of Herceg-Bosna expressed on the 18th of November, 1991, in Grude, taking the historic decision to establish the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, which serves as a legal basis for the entry of these territories into the Republic of Croatia." Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that. However, Your Honours, I have to comment. May I be allowed to comment upon what you have just read out and asked me whether I see it or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: It's a matter entirely for Their Honours to decide, whether you can comment at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Prosecutor, perhaps you can -- if you don't want to answer the question, perhaps you can pursue something else, if you don't think it's worthwhile.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: I'm entirely neutral as to that. The witness has asked for permission to speak. I don't want to deny him. It's for the Court to decide.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you wish to answer, give your answer, please, Witness, but briefly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it's incomprehensible, when it says here that a decision is being made which says: "... as a legal basis for the entry of these territories into the Republic of Croatia." I have never, ever attended a single meeting at which such a decision was made, and I don't think anybody else has. I don't know that this was ever voted on and decided on, because a statement of this kind, which is a nonsense and even at that time was never spoken aloud, I don't believe that we ever voted on that, that we ever decided that. I don't remember this conclusion. I don't remember any of the other things, but they are quite logical. However, this particular thing is totally illogical and incomprehensible.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not intervene before the witness answered. However, maybe the witness should be explained the nature of this document which is in front of me -- in front of him. You can see on the page before that Mr. Kostroman, which the Prosecutor started talking about, conveyed conclusions from some other sessions or meetings. Maybe we could take things one at a time. Maybe we could ask the witness whether he attended the session, whether the conclusions of some sort were made, whether he saw them or not, and then present them to him, because this is not meetings of -- this is not minutes of a meeting. These are just conclusions that were presented by Mr. Kostroman. I just wanted to say this, and maybe this will be of some assistance both to the Prosecutor and to the Trial Chamber to see what this is all about.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I never --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me. The interpreter, you wanted to translate --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: No, this was finished. This was the beginning of the witness's answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Okay. Your suggestions, Ms. Nozica, are fully sensible, but this is now for the Prosecution to decide what they want to ask him, and I think we should not interfere with that. But what the witness should be told: This document in no way speaks about any vote taken, about any decision taken. It only speaks about the foundation of an organisation which, in the opinion expressed here, could be a legal basis for any further decisions which, however, clearly have not been taken, and it's not said that they have been taken. So the nonsense is -- there's no nonsense in that sense. Excuse me, Mr. Laws. Please go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: I'm very grateful, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I apologise, I apologise. It was said that a meeting was held and that conclusions were arrived at. You can see it in the transcript, and this was the reason why I intervened. Minutes were taken. Maybe you can look at the document from the beginning. The minutes were taken by the following persons, and one of them was Mr. Bagaric, and it says further on: "Pursuant to the overall and quality debate, the following conclusions were arrived at ..." This means that these were conclusions that somebody made, and that's why I intervened, because I wanted to be sure that the witness participated in the meeting and whether he participated in the conclusions being made, and then conclusions should be listed from 1 to 10. This is my intervention, because this is an interpretation of some minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your colleagues have the floor, so ask your questions from the Prosecution, since the witness had told us under oath that he believes that never item 2 was discussed in his presence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Yes, we've heard that answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Dr. Bagaric, let's see if item 10 was ever discussed in your presence, shall we? That's at page 24. Can you see item 10, Doctor?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Item 10. It's at page 24. Do you have that paragraph, Doctor?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Item 4 is on page 22.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: No, item 10 on page 24.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Thank you. And there it says: "The legitimacy of Alija Izetbegovic, president of Bosnia-Herzegovina, to represent the Croatian people in public is hereby revoked." It goes on to say why. Do you remember being at a meeting where anything of that kind was said?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. Please bear with me. Yes. Well, yes, this was on the 27th of December, 1991. Absolutely, Your Honours, I don't remember any such conclusion. However, I would still be willing to understand this conclusion which was brought at that time, because that was the time after the Serb side set to fire, destroy, and kill the entire Croatian village of Ravno in Herzegovina, and then when one of the members of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina, not the president himself, when he said that this was not his war, that he was not going to take part in it. I was one of the deputies in the Parliament of Bosnia and Herzegovina at the time. I was elected during the first multi-party elections in 1990. I personally objected to such a position taken by Mr. Izetbegovic because he was representing the Bosniak Muslim people and in a certain way he represented the entire Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. However, at that time he was not representing the Croatian interests. I personally, at a meeting in Sarajevo, in the Parliament, and there are a lot of people who can testify to that, I asked Mr. Alija Izetbegovic, President, Sir, I would like to perceive you as my own president as well, and in order to be able to do that, I would have to have you represent our interests as well, and so on and so forth. So one of the attendees of the meeting was also Father Ferdo Vlasic, and I remember that meeting clearly. That meeting was a very informal meeting, and that person, during the time of communism, Your Honours, spent about 18 years in prison. He was a true Croatian and Herzegovinian Mandela. Together with Alija Izetbegovic, he was in prison. I asked him to get in touch with the president at the time, because I was just one of the deputies who issued very important documents for Bosnia and Herzegovina, and I wanted him to -- well, if you so wish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Dr. Bagaric, I've waited patiently for you to answer the question, but now we're talking about things that are a long way from this meeting, and I'm asking you --

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But they have a lot of bearing, a lot. No, I have to -- I have to react here. I have to react. This is -- but this is not true, this is not correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you consider this very close to the matter. The Prosecution think this is not relevant or very far away from it. Wait until the other questions are asked so that we can see what the position -- here you have spoken quite a while, and we have to understand the problems in this matter. We didn't know that you, yourself, had spoken in Parliament in Sarajevo to President Izetbegovic, so this is now in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Dr. Bagaric, we're going to spend a little time, you and I, this afternoon, and if it comes to it, tomorrow as well. At the end of that, you're going to be given a chance by Ms. Nozica to explain the things that remain to be explained. All right? You're not going to be deprived of an opportunity to speak. But in the meantime, I'm going to be asking you, I hope, some quite clear questions, and it's going to help me, and perhaps you as well, if we can just try and stick to answers that reflect those questions. Is that all right with you? Thank you very much. Now, this document that we have been looking at is, as I showed you at the very beginning, a tape-recording that was made on the 27th of December of 1991, in which matters that had been discussed at a meeting in Tomislavgrad in December -- 23rd of December, 1991, were read, and at page 19, we can see how the reading begins. Can you see, in the middle of the page, it's Mate Boban speaking, and he says: "I would like to ask that the conclusions be read and then perhaps raise some points for discussion and arrive at the truth from the region itself, that is, from the people, rather than airing my opinion or anybody else's." And Mr. Tudjman says: "All right. Please continue. Please introduce yourself for the record." And then Mr. Kostroman starts to read. He introduces himself, and over the page he says what he's reading; an excerpt from the minutes. All right? And this is where we started with you, as you now believe it is, present at the meeting whilst these matters are discussed. So far, Dr. Bagaric, do you and I agree?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. You are reading from page 19 in Croatian; is that so?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: What I just read to you is page 19 in the Croatian, and in the middle of the page President Tudjman asks Mr. Kostroman to introduce himself for the record, and he says: "I am Ignac Kostroman, secretary of the Croatian --"

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Tudjman, you're saying Tudjman?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Yes. [Overlapping speakers]. It's the 27th of December. It's a meeting presided over by Mr. Tudjman at which the minutes from the meeting in Tomislavgrad are read. I apologise if that hasn't been made clear enough to you so far, but that is the position.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: God, himself, would not be able to understand this.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Well, Dr. Bagaric, I'm looking around the room, and -- I suspect that everybody here understands it and that you do too, so let's not waste time with speculating about God's abilities. The 23rd of December meeting was one at which you were present, in which -- in which, Dr. Bagaric, people were outlining their views so far as they related to Herceg-Bosna and what it was intended to do; that's the position, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Try and help us. We have a document here, a document of 127 pages, and the Prosecution communicated to us some parts of it. But as I understand the problem, there is a meeting on the 27th of December, presided over by Mr. Tudjman, and a delegation which is from Bosnia-Herzegovina, and this meeting is in Zagreb, it's held in Zagreb. And during this meeting, and the Prosecution will tell me if I'm right, one mentions a meeting which took place a few days before on the 23rd of December, that is to say, four days earlier, in Tomislavgrad, and during that meeting you were personally present on the 23rd of December. And during this meeting of the 23rd of December, apparently, there are several points or items which were on the agenda which were discussed. This is how this document features, which in fact contains two things; one meeting of the 27th of December, during which there is the reading of a meeting of the 23rd of December. Do you understand a bit better the problem?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Precisely, that's what I didn't understand, because I was confused by -- how come Tudjman is suddenly in Tomislavgrad? I thank you for this clarification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. And in the 27th of December meeting, among the attendees you have Tudjman, Boban, and possibly others, but that we do not know, and apparently you were not in Zagreb on the 27th of December. Prosecutor, I don't know if I managed to shed light on this for everyone, because this is somewhat complicated.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: You understand the position now, Dr. Bagaric, and the true position is this: At that meeting, the intention of Boban and others, so far as Herceg-Bosna was concerned, was discussed. And you were there, and I'm going to suggest to you that you knew full well what the aims of Mate Boban and others were.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My answer is no, because you said that Mr. Boban had expressed certain intentions. I don't remember the term you used, but I didn't understand it. I was an MP, a deputy in the Parliament, and as a deputy I attended certain meetings that were related to the organisation of the defence of the Croatian people, and at that time also of the Muslim Bosniak people. Such meetings I attended quite frequently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, for the Prosecution this is -- this document is a very important item, because it's in the indictment, it's in the pre-trial brief. Item -- in item number 2, it's clearly written that the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna somehow confirms that it wants to enter, so to say, the Republic of Croatia. This was besides expressed on the 18th of November, 1991. Apparently you did attend that meeting. So if you say that this was never discussed, we have an issue, because it would mean that this document was forged, so either you lie or the document lies. So do you understand that what you're saying is of the utmost importance, because according to the document that we have, there was this debate where there was yourself, Kostroman, Boban, Kordic, et cetera. So there were many of you, and this issue, which is paramount for the Prosecutor's case, is debated -- presented, debated, and adopted. Earlier on, you said it wasn't, so I'm getting back to you. Are you sure this was never discussed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I said that I did attend one meeting in Tomislavgrad, and I suppose this is the meeting, which was also attended by those people from this group that we have referred to here. However, I can't say that each and every of these points were not discussed, but I don't remember. I say with full responsibility I don't remember discussion on this point, and especially that this conclusion was made, because from that point of view it was dumb and unclear, and even more so from today's point of view. But I personally don't remember it, anyhow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You can carry on, Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: 2.51.15[Previous translation continues]... you don't remember it. I'm going to have to suggest to you that it's quite something to forget, when you're at a meeting and fellow politicians and leaders are talking about acceding to Croatia and revoking the authority of Mr. Izetbegovic. That's quite something to slip your mind, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are not right, Mr. Prosecutor, because there are two things involved here. It is one thing to recall Mr. Izetbegovic at the time from representing Croats politically, and it is another thing to take a decision to accede. Looking from the point of view of that time, I quite understand that dissatisfaction was expressed about Mr. Izetbegovic, and there might have been even public releases to that effect, but as far as this conclusion is concerned, I don't agree that there was any discussion of this nature. I don't remember that, at least, and I'm stating that before this Court with full responsibility and before God.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Bagaric. I'm not sure whether you have heard and understood what I have told you earlier this afternoon. If you look at this text, this text is not a decision to join Croatia. You say there was no decision taken to join Croatia, and you are quite right. That is not what this text says. This text says, We founded the Croat Community of Herceg-Bosna, which would be a legal basis from which eventually to jump into Croatia, but it is not a decision to jump and to join. Maybe if you reconsider this, you can agree that or remember that this was actually said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you're right, Your Honour. However, I really don't recall this, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Dr. Bagaric, I'm going to suggest to you simply this: that you were not in any doubt at all about what the aims of Mate Boban and Herceg-Bosna were. They were nationalist aims. They were going to accede to Croatia. That is the simple truth of the matter, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That would mean, in that case, that for me, as a representative, as a deputy, Mate Boban was God, to whom we did not dare say a word or oppose. That means that Ivan Bagaric, as an MP in the Parliament of Bosnia and Herzegovina, was a "yes" man. But as far as Ivan Bagaric was concerned, that was never the case, and that includes that particular point in time. Whether Mate Boban had certain intentions or not, I don't know. Possibly. But nobody ever officially presented that to me, nor did I ever think, Your Honours, that this would happen, simply because it was impossible to realise, it was impossible to implement, and I was aware of that even then.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Well, whether it was possible or not, it was certainly going to be something that would cause a great deal of displeasure among many Muslims in the population that was claimed as Herceg-Bosna, was it not?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, no, because that region that proclaimed itself Herceg-Bosna was a region which, when the state had collapsed or even when it was obvious that it would eventually collapse, we wanted to defend ourselves however we could, and therefore we assumed certain autonomy so that we could take decisions in order to be able to organise defence. I was there, and you weren't. It was in keeping with the constitution at the time. You said that I was a politician. I am primarily a doctor, but I accept that I was acting as a politician then. You had the right, in defence, to join others. That sort of joinder was legitimate. It was the will of elected representatives, and I did participate in organising the defence of areas where Croats were the majority and where there were also Muslim populations, in order to oppose an overwhelming enemy, which were the Serbs. Later, there were victims, of course, due to the aggression that was caused by Serbs, by the Serbian Army. That is the truth. I lived it, and my family suffered through it and paid the price, and my brother, whom we mentioned yesterday, got killed defending Bosnia and Herzegovina, as a volunteer who had come from Germany via Croatia, and laid his life there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: We heard about that and we're sorry for that, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you've provided a lengthy answer to the Prosecution's question, but I'm interested in the following, because this is the first time we've had a member of Parliament, who was at the Sarajevo Parliament. What you've just said today was said by you in the Parliament, was it, by you or by others, and do we have written records of addresses by members of Parliament on the very topics you're dealing with today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've always said that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but as a member of the Sarajevo Parliament, when you take the floor, is there a record, is there a transcript of what you say? For example, you said, Well, I challenge, or, I address Izetbegovic. When you asked that question in Parliament, perhaps you provided an answer. Is there a written record of your question, and was that answer also recorded, and have other MPs like you developed that thesis on the issue of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Mr. President, thank you for giving me this opportunity to answer this question, because I think it's very important. I think you really need to understand this for any further discussion. I am really in a hurry to go back to my obligations, but this is more important than my obligations and engagements or anything else. It was a time when Serbs openly assaulted Croatia, shelled both Dubrovnik and Vukovar, and other towns, and it was obvious that war would begin in Bosnia-Herzegovina. At that time, I sat in the same Parliament as Alija Izetbegovic, Stjepan Kljujic, and Radovan Karadzic. Radovan Karadzic, I stress. I rose to the rostrum on one occasion, and there must be a record of that, because it was obvious that the war would begin, that Serbs were preparing for war. They were doing the job in Croatia and preparing a war in Bosnia and Herzegovina. It was evident and plain for everyone to see. So I came to the rostrum and I said, You are there. Radovan Karadzic, representing Serbs; Stjepan Kljujic, Croats; Alija Izetbegovic, Bosniaks; come up here and say that there would be no war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay, I've given you plenty of time to answer, but my question was fairly specific. Is there a written record of the debates in the Parliament in Sarajevo? And you say, I don't know. Do you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps absolutely --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are you saying it is possible?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, I can't know. I have no way of knowing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not sure whether these records are still in existence, but it would be very important to look at them to see just who said what in Parliament. But I am proud of what I said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you ought to know the following: In this court, the procedure is not set by the Judges. It's up to the parties to provide evidence, the Prosecution, the Defence. Had I been running this procedure, the first thing I would have done would have been to look at the transcript of the debates in the Sarajevo Parliament, with Karadzic, Izetbegovic, yourself, Kljujic, et cetera, but I do not have such documents. Please carry on, Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: We're going to move away from that meeting to the next year, Dr. Bagaric, September of 1992, when you were offered a job within the Herceg-Bosna Ministry of Defence to be the head of the Health Sector. September of 1992. All right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which document is that?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: You don't need a document for it. It's 2D00702. We don't need one. You know you were appointed in September of 1992.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Counsel, I'm sorry. We haven't heard your question yet, but I still want to be precise. It wasn't a ministry. It was the Department of Defence. I would appreciate precision in the names of various agencies. It was not a ministry, at least not in that month.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: I don't expect that anybody was misled.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: In September of 1992, Dr. Bagaric, you were approached and offered a post within the Herceg-Bosna Department of Defence; all right? Who offered you that job? Who was it who got in touch with you?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours, but I really cannot give such short answers here. I was an MP to the Parliament of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and I was offered the post of head of the Health Sector much, much earlier. I've already said that we doctors had organised a medical service much earlier than September. Local representatives in Sarajevo and others offered it to me when we were organising the defence of the region. It was not actually an offer, it was an appointment, but that appointment was already in place. Nobody was offering it to me. This was just a renaming. When other appointments were made, I was appointed to this post. That much is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: All right, Dr. Bagaric. Let me ask the question more broadly. Who was it who first invited you to take any sort of job, role, position of responsibility, within any part of the Herceg-Bosna apparatus of state? Do you follow that question? You were a doctor and you were a member of Parliament, and then somebody asked you to become involved in some way with Herceg-Bosna, and I'm asking you who it was.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those were my colleagues, MPs -- representatives, that is, and there were over 40 in Sarajevo. It was at one of our meetings when we were talking and when we were aware that the war would indeed start, and we discussed who could do what. And I, being a doctor, they said that since I was an MP and a doctor, it would be good for me to make preparations for assistance to the wounded and such.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Would you please try now to answer the question, giving us perhaps some names of the people within Herceg-Bosna who asked you to become involved in organising the Health Sector? Just some names; not your colleagues. Who were they?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were doctors, Dr. Ivan Sarac, Marko Frankovic, then a gentleman -- I believe Boskovic is the name. I haven't seen him in a long while, also a doctor. Then a gentleman by the name of Markovic, also a medical doctor. Ante Bosniak, a dentist from Citluk. Nevinka [phoen] --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: You were able to give us a number of names, and that helps us a lot. The first is Dr. Ivan Sarac, who was also at the meeting in Tomislavgrad in December of 1991 and, as you said, went on to become the senior official within the Health Department. But these were people at a similar level to you, weren't they? Who was it above you who was able to give you the very important job that you told us about yesterday?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not a job; it was a duty. I did not get employed there, and I did not receive a salary. It was a duty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, the Prosecutor is asking you a technical question. He's asking who appointed you or offered you the job. Either you know or you don't. If it's Mr. Stojic, you say it's Mr. Stojic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, formally speaking, I don't remember. I don't know. It was not Mr. Stojic. I don't know who it was, who formally did it, but I know that Mate Boban as well is one of the MPs in the Parliament of Bosnia and Herzegovina, because I met up with Boban at the Parliament and he was probably at the same meetings, so it could have been him. I don't remember if anyone formally appointed me, but as I said, it was a duty, not a job.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Yes, and we all appreciate the difference that you're trying to draw, I'm sure. But is the short answer that it was Mate Boban? Can we not just cut to the chase? Isn't that the position? Mate Boban asked you to do this job, end of story. That's it, isn't it, Dr. Bagaric?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no. I was an MP, on an equal footing with other MPs. Therefore, it transpired from a discussion among MPs who were also physicians. Mate Boban could not have made the offer because he's not a physician.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Dr. Bagaric, I really don't want to spend very much more time on this, but you don't have to be a physician to appoint somebody who's going to assist Bruno Stojic in that way, do you? It's not a sensible answer that you've given to this Trial Chamber, is it? And you're a sensible man, Doctor.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you can be satisfied with my answer that it could have been Mate Boban, I've given it to you. It could have been Mate Boban, as far as the formal appointment is concerned, but I'm trying to explain how the proposal came about.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: You give it and you take it away. Not interested in that. I'm interested in your appointment, and you give the name Mate Boban, but then you want to take it away again, and it's just wasting our time. Mate Boban gave you the job, and he gave you the job because you were a trusted person who shared with him many of the goals of Herceg-Bosna. That's the simple answer, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: All right. Well, I'm going to suggest to you, before we turn to look at some of the details of the evidence that you've given in the last two days, that that is what lies behind you, as a doctor. You are a doctor and a politician, and you are a politician of a particular character in 1991 and 1992 and 1993, a loyal and trusted politician, intimate with Boban and with others who were key to Herceg-Bosna. That's you, Dr. Ivan Bagaric, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I was not loyal to Mate Boban. I was loyal to the people who elected me, that is, the Croats of Tomislavgrad municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: When you gave evidence on Monday -- I'm going to turn away from that now, and I'm going to come back to it at the end of what you and I have to say to one another. When you gave evidence on Monday, Doctor, you said that when you visited Sovici/Doljani, you said, To my great satisfaction, no crimes had been committed against the civilians there, and that this was confirmed by the Muslims to whom you spoke. Do you giving that answer?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember the gist of my answer, but I'm not sure I said that exactly in that way. I'm not sure. Why? Because Muslim commanders accused us, and that includes me, as a physician, saying, Your army, your troops raped our women, victimised our civilians. But eventually when we got there, we saw that it was not like that. I'm not saying that not a single civilian was killed. At that time, I wasn't really aware. But when we came there, the people whom we found there and that expressed their satisfaction, speaking to us and to the Muslim representatives, including Mr. Halilovic, and we went there and we were satisfied that the truth was not exactly what we had been told.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you to pause there, if you wouldn't mind, Doctor, because the question that I asked you was whether you recalled giving the answer that it was to your great satisfaction that no crimes had been committed against civilians and that the Muslims had confirmed that. And I think you and I are agreed that that was the gist of what you were saying. It may not be the absolute word-for-word answer, but that's the gist of it. And you gave evidence to a very similar effect at this Tribunal in the case of Tuta Stela, did you not?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I testified in the case of Tuta Stela about the so-called general circumstances. I don't remember that this was discussed. However, if this had been discussed, then my -- the only answer I could have provided was along these lines, because that's how things transpired. And I will never forget what happened and how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Well, it was discussed when you gave evidence, and I'm putting to you, and maybe you'll just agree --

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: -- that the gist of what you were saying in the Tuta Stela case was the same; that you went to Sovici, Doljani, and that you spoke to people, and you were pleased to find out that really there were no complaints against the HVO. That's what it came down to in your evidence here on Monday, and very much the same thing some six years ago. All right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, it is possible. If I was saying anything at the time, then I would have been saying the same things I'm saying today.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: That's right. And the six years that elapsed since the Trial Chamber in that case delivered its judgement, have you troubled at any stage to have a look at that judgement and to see whether it might be that your state of knowledge of events in Sovici/Doljani is inadequate?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I had testified about general circumstances. I did not testify about Tuta or Stela [as interpreted] because I did not know them. Of course, I never investigated the --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Did I ask you that? Did I once ask you that? Just have a look at the question.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you did. You did, you asked me that.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise to the Prosecutor. The witness is answering the Prosecutor's question, and he should be let to do so. His last sentence was that he didn't know these people and he never investigated, and he was about to answer your question, but he should have been allowed to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, the Prosecutor has asked you a very specific question. He says six years ago you testified, there was a judgement, and the Prosecutor is asking you whether you read the judgement, and, if so, if this changed or would change your conclusions. So it's quite specific.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am sorry. I never read the judgement, and nothing can modify my memory and my feelings, because my feelings are even more important than what I remember, the feeling that I had when I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: To say that nothing could modify your feelings about it is --

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Don't interrupt me, please, Doctor, while I'm just finishing my question. I'm doing my level best not to interrupt you when your answers run to many, many lines. But you've just said nothing can modify your memory or your feelings, and I'm going to ask you whether historical fact is not capable of altering the way that you view events in Sovici/Doljani.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. You want to represent me as a person without feelings. You said that I had just said that nothing can change my feelings. I did not say that. If a crime had been committed, and I did not know about it, I would still feel comfortable, this is not correct. I said that nothing could change my memory and the feeling that I had at the time. I experienced what I did, and I was happy to see that nothing of the kind described by the Muslim commanders had happened there. Here, every word is being weighed, and for my own sake, for the sake of this Trial Chamber and this Tribunal, I would like to provide a very clear answer to every question of yours. Please, stop putting words into my mouth if I never said them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Later, perhaps you'll get a chance to check, but I used your words, not my own. Dr. Bagaric --

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: -- at paragraph 238, the Trial Chamber describes a number of events that had taken place in Sovici and Doljani. They say that the Muslim houses in the area were burnt to make sure that there would be no return of the Muslim population. They say that Muslim religious sites, like the mosques in the area, were systematically destroyed. All right? And that had taken place, the destruction -- just wait a moment. The destruction of the houses and the destruction of the mosque in Sovici had taken place at the time that you arrived with the joint mission on 4th/5th of May. Did you see houses that had been razed to the ground and rubble where the mosque had been?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see that, Your Honour. I arrived in an UNPROFOR vehicle, under protection. I was brought in front of the school. We had a meeting there, and nothing of the sort -- I don't remember having seen any of that. If I'd seen any such thing, I would have remembered. I am saying what I heard at the meeting from the people who were also attending that meeting and who had been detained in that school. There were detained Muslim Bosniaks, and we spoke to them, and this is what I am talking about. Later on, we got back into the APC and we left. And as for the area that the Prosecutor is mentioning, whether something of the kind happened immediately after we had left, I don't know that, either. I'm not saying that all that the Prosecutor is mentioning could not have happened there. However, at that meeting I don't remember anybody having raised that as a problem. I don't remember having seen anything of the kind, any of us. The most important thing for me was that the civilians who were there told us that there had been no mass killings, large-scale rapes, and all the other things that I feared I would possibly find there and I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: The people that you were talking about in your last answer, the people with whom you had a discussion about mass killings and large-scale rapes, they were the villagers of Sovici/Doljani and the surrounding area who by that stage had been held captive in the schoolhouse for more than a fortnight. Are you seriously saying they had no complaints about the HVO?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise to my learned friend. I believe that there has been a misunderstanding of the previous answer of the witness. He said that the people did not complain of mass murders, rapes on a large scale, and I therefore believe that part of my learned friend's question, where he says that the witness discussed mass murders with the people, and rapes, is simply not fair, because this contains a statement that the witness never uttered.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Well, may I answer that? May I answer that? On Monday of this week, and we can all check the transcript, this witness gave evidence that the Muslim population of Sovici, in the schoolhouse, were complaining about their own side not having sent them sufficient help. They were complaining that the army, the ARBiH, hadn't sent them the help they wanted, and not a word about any complaint to do with the HVO. The question, I submit, is a fair one, and I'm going to repeat it, if I may.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: There were no complaints, then, about the HVO; do we have that right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe you misunderstood me. If we're going to be fair, completely fair, I see what you're saying. It's not that they complained that the army had not sent them any help. They complained because they had been betrayed by the army commanders. And I'm paraphrasing. Somebody told them, Don't worry, launch an attack. Maybe not an attack, but in military terms, something, We will then come to your aid. And this didn't happen. I'm talking about a conflict, and it was not the insufficient help because somebody had attacked somebody else. The civilians were very dissatisfied with the Muslim commanders, with Halilovic, and I don't remember that they ever expressed any dissatisfaction with anybody else, or maybe I wasn't there if such dissatisfaction was expressed. From what I could hear, there was no such dissatisfaction at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: You've just expressed again the view that I was putting to you and which Ms. Alaburic suggested might be unfair. I think we can all see that that is your view of things and that the question that I put to you was not unfair. No complaints about the HVO, and so you come here in 2009 and say what you said about your great satisfaction there were no complaints and no crimes committed against civilians. The people that you spoke to --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm going to object to that. Is that commentary, or is that evidence, or is he summing up? I think what his view is --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: I'm trying to draw the strands together from an extremely difficult and complex web of answers that the witness has given.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, he can do that in his final brief, not during the --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: No, because I've got another question to ask.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, I believe that last commentary was commentary for final brief and not part of a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Prosecutor, please ask your questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: The people who you were speaking to in that schoolhouse, who were prisoners of the HVO, were later to be put onto buses and transferred to an area near to Gornji Vakuf, and I'm going to ask you to look at an HVO document with me, please. It's P02372. It's a little bit further on in the same binder that you were given earlier today. Do you have that document, Dr. Bagaric?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: You can see that it's over the name of somebody called Marko Rozic and that it is from the Jablanica municipality defence office, and it calls itself a decision. It's dated the 13th of May of 1993, and under Roman I, it says: "All movable property and real estate of the Muslims that emigrated shall be considered to be spoils of war and it shall belong to the HZ-HB Croatian Defence Council." Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that item.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: And this Trial Chamber has heard evidence of villagers from that locality who were transferred, and who came back, and who found that their property had been taken, and that was being done, Doctor, in order to ensure that the Muslim population would not want to return. And the question that I'm going to ask you is: Having looked at some of this evidence and that document, do you want to change your feelings about Sovici/Doljani or is the position, as you said a while ago, that nothing could change your view of it?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, objection to the question, because the witness --

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this time -- this type of examination, Your Honours, I have a right to object. This is an inappropriate questioning. The conclusions that the Prosecutor tries to draw only irritate the witness. If we want to irritate the witness, if we want to aggravate the witness, if we don't want the witness to answer the questions -- I can see Judge Trechsel not approving with what I'm saying, but I will still bring my point home. He did not say that he could not change his feelings about what happened. He explained very clearly that the feeling that he had at the meeting and what he learned at the meeting at the time cannot be changed. The witness is now being portrayed as ruthless and insensitive to things that might have happened and he did not know about. This is an inappropriate type of examination, and that's why I'm objecting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Nozica, Ms. Nozica, your intervention is totally inappropriate for the following reason: The witness has given his position. Since the beginning, he is not changing this position. All right, very well. We have understood very well his point. The Prosecution, who is doing his job, he has his own thesis about it, and he shows a document to the witness. Everybody can read it, everybody can see it. Muslims have seen their house taken by the HVO. The Prosecution tells him to look at this document, Does this document change the way you feel about the events? That's all. He answers, No, or he can say, I'm discovering this now. This is the debate. You are objecting because you don't like this. I will make you note, Ms. Nozica, that during the four hours you have been using, never the Prosecution has asked for the floor. He let you do your job, and you did it quite well. Let him do his job properly, and the Judges will decide.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I apologise. I accept your position and your opinion, but then obviously the Trial Chamber has not understood what the witness actually said. The witness said, I have feelings about the fact -- facts and what I heard at the meeting. He never -- and what I saw on that day. He never said that nothing could change his feelings if there were things that he never heard or saw, and that's why I'm intervening. Now he is being asked whether this could change his feelings, and he said that his feelings arise from what he, himself, heard and saw, and that's why I intervened. Otherwise, I would not have intervened, because I understood from the Prosecutor's questions that he is trying to portray the witness in a completely different light.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: If I may reply to that, please, just briefly. First of all, I'm not remotely trying to irritate the witness. The witness has, on two occasions at this Tribunal, given a version of events at Sovici/Doljani which the Prosecution say is from an entirely fictional world, and we're allowed to address that. That's what I'm doing, and I'm going to move on to the events of May, if I may.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I could just be heard for one second.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I answer the question, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I could be heard for just one second, because I think the problem is, if I could just summarise it, is that the Prosecution is mischaracterising the witness's testimony and that he's using that as a predicate in order to formulate his next question, and that is, if you go back and you listen to it very carefully, look at the transcript, it is exactly -- it is a technique that is used by common-law lawyers when they want to trick a witness, and this is not the purpose of this procedure. So I would appreciate it if my learned colleague would be very careful in not mischaracterising the witness's testimony when he sums up and uses it as a predicate, as a basis in formulating a following question, in looping.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Well, I'd respectfully submit it's hard to know, then, what the purpose of calling this witness to deal with Sovici/Doljani was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Prosecutor, even under the assumption that you were trying to trick the witness, you have professional Judges on the Bench; therefore, it is not possible. I shall not enter -- I will not enter in this question. I listen to the question, I listen to the answer, I watch the witness, and this is how I proceed. And I have the documents in front of me. Therefore, Witness, you are a doctor, you're a deputy, a member of Parliament. You have high functions. You understand the meaning of the question from the Prosecution, and under oath you have been with UNPROFOR in Sovici with Halilovic and General Petkovic. You were in this school, you saw the people who were there. You got back into the vehicle and you left. That's what you told us, and I am just noting what you are giving is your own version. The Prosecution just said that he takes issue with what you say. Therefore, this is clear. What do you say now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I actually did not answer the Prosecutor's question -- the last Prosecutor's question before the interventions of the counsel. He asked me whether I would change my feelings after having seen the decision, and it is exactly as the counsel put it. I said very clearly that nothing can change the feeling and the memory that I had at the time, there and then, so many years back, because my memory is still vivid. Why? Because I was afraid that the stories were true, because if they had been, I would have been sad, it would have been terrible. People would have been killed, and that would be just the beginning of a long and sad story. However, when I see this order, this decision, and if things were as they are described herein, which I don't know anything about, then of course any normal person -- I don't know whether this decision is militarily correct or whether there is -- it is correct to take somebody's house as a spoils of war, but I believe that nobody's house can be spoils of war. And of course, I'm sorry if things happened in the way described in here, in this decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I would just like to make one observation. I think in these many objections, Ms. Alaburic was just talked down by Ms. Nozica, but I think you have not -- you're not insisting.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, let me just say that my learned friend Nozica has priority because Dr. Bagaric is her witness. That's why I retreated. But I really wanted to say exactly what my learned friend Nozica said, so there's no need for me to add anything to her words. She summed it up pretty well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Fine. I fully agree to the reaction of our President of the Chamber, but there is one point which I think is to be criticised in the question of the Office of the Prosecutor, of Mr. Law, and it's on page 31-32, where you said, Mr. Law: "And this was being done, Doctor, in order to ensure that the Muslim population would not want to return." And I think there you're going a bit beyond what is in the document and giving interpretation which is yours, and it's not correct, I think, to put that to the witness as if it were an accepted fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: I fully accept what you say, Your Honour. The Prosecution say that's the inference to be drawn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: In the following month, Dr. Bagaric, May of 1993, large numbers of Muslim residents of Mostar were taken from their homes and put into the Heliodrom. You know that, do you not?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know of the Heliodrom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you are not answering precisely the question. The question of the Prosecution is fundamental. He is asking you, Do you know, are you aware of the fact that people were taken to the Heliodrom? And you answer, I know the Heliodrom. So the question was much more precise. He wanted to know if you knew -- if you were aware of the fact that people had been taken to the Heliodrom. This is the substance of the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I knew of the situation. I knew of the final situation, which was that people had been brought to the Heliodrom, a lot of people had been brought there, a lot of Muslims and Bosniaks. Under what conditions, under what circumstances, I don't know, because I never saw that with my own eyes, and I cannot answer the question in any other way. I know of the Heliodrom, I knew of the Heliodrom, and I know that people had been brought there, that people were there. I know that, and that's the only fact I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: We're going to need to go into closed session just for a moment, please, if we may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, please, closed session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Dr. Bagaric, Witness 2D-AB had a memory of it being you who had first asked him to go to the Heliodrom immediately after the arrest that had taken place in the early part of May in Mostar. He remembered it as you, Dr. Bagaric, who had told him to go down there. Does your memory accord with his?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If he said so, I will agree. I was with him almost every day, and we provided each other with instructions or commands -- or, rather, not commands, we did not command each other. If that's his testimony, then I can agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: If you can remember for us, please, how you came to learn that large numbers of people been detained at the Heliodrom. Who was it who told you so that you could tell Witness 2D-AB that he should go to the Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, one could say that you could not hide the fact that a city is ablaze. It was a notorious fact. My colleagues, doctors, were talking about that. And if we are talking about the same thing, it was the beginning of an open conflict in Mostar with the BH Army on the one side and the HVO on the other side, so we're talking about major developments in Mostar at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: I understand that, but the position was this: People had been taken from their homes, including, as this Trial Chamber has seen, large numbers of doctors, put in the Heliodrom, and you appear to have said to 2D-AB that he should go there, and you agree that he may well be right. Were you saying that that was just from your general information, as somebody who was in Mostar at the time, or was the position that somebody asked you to go there or, rather, to send 2D-AB there?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that anybody asked me to do that. I repeat, it was a major development. I can't be sure, after so much time, when I was there, but I believe that it was significantly later. I spoke about that yesterday -- the day before yesterday. I really can't remember, sir, how this transpired. I can't remember the details of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: You also told us that when he came back, and he had found it an upsetting visit, when he came back he told you and other people in the Health Sector what he had seen there; do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I really can't remember that specific moment, but I believe that I was provided with a full picture, that I was provided actually not a full picture but a general picture of the situation over there, about the needs to intervene, to monitor the situation, as it were, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: He recalls that it was in the Health Sector, having come back from the Heliodrom, and he was telling people, including you, what he had seen, he told us what he had seen, that he had seen people who were very afraid, people who didn't know why they had been put into prison, and people who were overwhelmingly Muslims. Now, I want you to cast your mind back for us, please, Dr. Bagaric, because that's an extraordinary turn of events in the life of any city, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said that this was the beginning of an open conflict in Mostar. It was a big event, something that I had feared all the time. Everything pointed to that, and it did happen, and this was one of the consequences of that development.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: The question that I'm asking you -- the question that I'm asking you is there for everybody to see; that he recalls that he was telling people in the Health Sector what he had seen.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: I'll give way to Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Perhaps it may be good, because of the guidance previously provided by the Trial Chamber, for the gentleman to read from the transcript what exactly was said, and give us a page number, and what have you. That this way, the gentleman would actually hear the words, and this may be of some assistance. I don't mean to interrupt or disrupt.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Well, I think we all have the general --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Procedure, sir. We have procedures here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. It's time for a break. During the break, Prosecutor, you can seek and look for the exact transcript of 2B [as interpreted] so everyone is aware of what was said. So we'll have a 20-minute break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Prosecutor, so I'm sure that you have found the exact words uttered by Witness 2B [as interpreted], so, please, you can read them out to Mr. Bagaric.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: The transcript is at page 37602, and it's a question posed by Judge Antonetti at line 9, the question starting at 15: "When you left the Heliodrom, did you tell your superiors, I'm going to the prison -- I'm going to the Heliodrom, I've met people whom I knew, and these people didn't know why they had been detained? Did you tell that to your superiors, and if you did, what did they then tell you?" And the witness said: "First of all, of course I did tell them. That was my duty, that was my duty to tell them, and when I went down there, as you've already heard, well, Dr. Bagaric told me to go down there." And, Dr. Bagaric, you were Witness 2D-AB's superior, were you not?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: So I hope that we're all agreed. I want to ask you whether you agree with his recollection that when he came back from the Heliodrom, he reported to you about what he had seen.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't agree or disagree with his recollection, but I can say that if he says it happened like that, that it was a man who performed his task professionally and with whom I cooperated very closely, so I have reason to believe that whatever he said, it is roughly true or exactly true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Doctor, when I asked the question to that witness, what I had in mind was the situation of your Muslim colleagues, and I asked that question and I thought I knew that he had colleagues who had been detained, so it was quite important. Let's imagine we Judges here find some of our colleagues have been arrested. It's quite an important event, which you do remember. So when you heard that your Muslim colleagues were arrested, it must have struck you, you as well as all the Croatian doctors, and you must have asked yourselves, well, why did they arrest them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I mean, I have to be perfectly precise and honest. At that time, at that moment in time in the beginning of May, I am not sure that I already knew that the doctors were there. (redacted) had told me, then it's probably true. However, I don't recall that moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Hold on. We need to redact this, because you've pronounced the name of the witness. And since there were protective measures, I'd like to ask the Registrar to draw an order. You can proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. So I suppose, although I'm not sure, that my colleagues who were detained at the time were Mr. Stranjak and Mr. Hadzic, I believe. And I'm not sure whether they were formally at the HVO or not and what the circumstances were, but I know for sure that these physicians were absolutely certainly at that centre later, and with them - how shall I put it? - we did an important job there, because they remained to work at Heliodrom. And for every physician, and certainly me, when we heard the news first, it must have been unpleasant.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Well, I'm going to come to doctors in just a moment, but I was asking you about when the Witness 2D-AB came back and reported to you, and you said that, well, you're not sure, but if he said that that was right, it was probably right, but you don't recall at the moment. That's what you said --

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... line 18.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: If you'd look in the bundle, please, at the document P02315. Do you have that document, Doctor?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: You can see that it's over the name of a colleague of yours about whom you've already spoken, Dr. Ante Kvesic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Ante Kvesic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: This is a list -- the heading of the document is a list of the employees of the Mostar HVO regional field hospital and their family members who were taken away from their flats. It's a list that contains 106 names. It would -- MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] My learned friend, I'm sorry, I'd like to say that we have the wrong document on the screen. Document 3315 is on the screen, and the Prosecutor wanted 2315. I've been warned from behind, and it's true we have the wrong document on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, P02315. I think the witness has the right document.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Were you aware, sir, of these people being detained at the Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite honestly, I don't remember this list, but I do know for sure that Dr. Kvesic, who was the director of the hospital, took care of that and he was in charge, and he knew what happened to all of the people. I don't know which of these people are doctors, although I see that some of them are, one, two, yes, and who were family members. And another reason why I'm not qualified to speak of this document is that at that time, due to a particular set of circumstances, I was not in Mostar on -- I was not in Mostar on the 11th of May. I was there on the 5th May, but at that time not. I think I was on the road. This was after my visit to Canada that had been arranged much earlier, and the procedure of getting the visa took quite a long time. So I spent quite a long time in Canada, and that was done in agreement with my colleagues and with my superiors. That's why I can't be qualified to speak of this. But I hold that if Dr. Kvesic signed it, I suppose that in this incident some doctors and family members were taken away, although I don't know, really.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Help me, please, Dr. Bagaric. Are you saying that you were or were not aware that in May of 1993, a large number of civilians in Mostar were arrested and taken to the Heliodrom? Were you aware of that in May of 1993 or were you not aware perhaps because you were in Canada or on the road?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said I was aware of that, of course I was. But I spoke of this document in particular dated 11th May, and I said I wasn't sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Hold on, Dr. Bagaric. Please be accurate. We find out, because I didn't know that you were in Canada in May. When did you go to Canada and when did you come back? When did you leave and when did you come back?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think -- I think, but I'm not sure, that sometime on the 15th, I had already arrived in Canada, and I stayed at least 20 days, at least; two days more or less, but that's the time-frame.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Which means that on the 9th, 10th and 11th of May, you were in the area, in the Mostar area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was in the area of Mostar when that first clash happened. I cannot tell you the exact date. If that was before the 15th, a few days before the 15th, then I certainly was there. Was it on the 9th?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But when, on May the 11th, Dr. Kvesic - sorry about the pronunciation - draws that report stating that there are 106 persons belonging to the medical profession, in the broad sense of the word, who were expelled from their flats and brought somewhere, we know that there are several doctors, and there are names, and there is the 12th and the 13th, et cetera, this is quite a significant event which affects the medical community, so you must have been informed on the 11th of May. It cannot be differently.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I've already said that I remember the incident, the event. I remember that some medical staff and family members were taken away. But this was signed -- this was dated on the 11th of May. It doesn't mean that the event happened on the 11th. I don't know when the document was created, but I know of the event.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Whenever you came to know about it, Dr. Bagaric, the position was that the HVO had been taking people who had not done anything wrong and had been putting them in a prison just outside Mostar; can we agree about that?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, people were certainly taken away and out of Mostar to Heliodrom. That is indisputable. That's my answer. But certainly, if you let me finish, I can't go into the guilt of -- guilt or innocence of any of these people, but I suppose certainly that a large number of these people could not have been guilty of anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: You don't -- you do not, in your heart, seriously believe, Dr. Bagaric, that of this list of 106 doctors and their family, and other medical staff, that we're dealing with a list of wrong-doers who had to be detained? You don't believe that at all, do you?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no, that's not true. I see these names. If it's true that these people were Mila, Maja, and the physicians, Safiqa [phoen], Azra, Latifa, I believe that they were not wrong-doers, that they had not done anything wrong. I'm saying that I can't be sure that some of these people did not do anything wrong. I don't know about that, in fact. I know of the event, I know that these things happened, that indeed physicians, and I'm talking primarily of physicians, were taken away to the camp, or rather the prison, or whatever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Doctor, if some, as you said, could have been wrong-doers, but I'd like to draw your attention to 32 and 37. Look at this. These are children. How do you account for this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't see this. Of course, children. But normally, Your Honours, I've already said if women were taken away, if children, as we see, were taken away, then certainly there could have been no reason, unless the reason was to protect those people from the conflict. That, I could understand. Of course, I could not understand it in the broader context, whatever reason was preferred.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: You were in this period, Dr. Bagaric, regularly meeting with Bruno Stojic?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite honestly, I don't remember meeting with him regularly at that time. I'm sorry, but could you help me? When was the first day of the conflict in that month? Was it the 5th, the 6th? What was the date of the open conflict in May?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
