utterances.text: I'm dealing now very specifically with Bruno Stojic; all right? I want you to focus on him for a moment. You told the Trial Chamber, either yesterday or the day before, that you had meetings with him as the need arose. Did you ever discuss with Bruno Stojic the events that had led to people being imprisoned in the Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that period, in that particular period from the date when it happened until this date, I certainly was unable to discuss it with him, because I was already away in Canada, as I told you. Certainly, later, when I came back, I not only talked to Bruno; I discussed it with many people.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Well, you'd have been back in June, you told us, and this would still have been a very big story in Mostar in June, these arrests. Heliodrom was to continue, as we're going to see, for many, many months after this. Did you at any stage have a conversation with Bruno Stojic about what was happening and why people were being detained in the Heliodrom prison?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I returned, I think this group of people had already been released, and as far as I remember -- or perhaps the majority had been released, so I don't remember any discussion with Bruno Stojic specifically on this topic, or anyone else, for that matter, because by the time I returned, I believe most of these people had been released. It was the initial period of that first conflict, and then things calmed down. The circumstances were no longer that dramatic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Well, as I think we are agreed, and as we're going to see, whatever the position with the doctors and their families might have been, the Heliodrom continued for many, many months, and I'm going to ask you the question again and give you another opportunity to answer it. During that time, did you ever have a conversation with Bruno Stojic about what had led to people being detained in the Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your question relates to the entire period, doesn't it, from the beginning of Heliodrom until the end?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: I used the word "ever." I hope it was clear to you. I've used it twice. Did you ever have a conversation -- just let me finish, and we'll get it absolutely clear. Did you ever have a conversation with him about this topic?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I did, I think, but I think I also spoke to a great number of people, not only Bruno Stojic. I must admit not too often, because we didn't meet very often, except at collegium meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: What did Bruno Stojic say about why people were in the Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't really interpret now what Bruno Stojic said, or what I said, or anyone else. However, I believe that my discussions related to the situation, such as this case, that things should be improved, redressed, to the best our ability to influence things, but the security situation was so disrupted in Mostar that you couldn't know what was -- what the right thing to do was and what to decide. I think that was the gist of whatever I could have discussed with Bruno Stojic or anyone else.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: I'll try that question one more time. You've said that you can't really interpret now what he said, or what you said, or anyone else. Can you help us at all with what Bruno Stojic said about why people were in the Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember specifically. It was an open conflict, and it was impossible to control the overall situation in the region or to protect either Muslims or Croats, because the hostility was open and deteriorating. I don't remember this detail specifically.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Is that going to be your answer to my question?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would, I would stick to that answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Did you know that there was a forced labour programme within the Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After my return from Canada, I think -- I think I went to Heliodrom for the first time sometime after my return from Canada and assessed the situation for the first time. I had heard by then, especially from reports by our physicians who were working there and from talking to them, that indeed there were certain incidents involving prisoners who were sent to perform certain jobs. With a certain delay, I did hear about these things, but I was not directly informed, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Your colleague, Dr. 2-AB [sic], has told this Trial Chamber that he suspected there was a forced labour programme, had suspicions about it, and that he told you about his suspicions, and the transcript is page 37648. And that would accord with your recollection, as you've just described it to us?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I repeat, I heard it from my colleagues, doctors. I can't say that it was him or any particular individual. These doubts existed, these suspicions existed. And these things happened to a certain extent, but I don't know on which scale and how often they happened. I don't know any particular details.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: He was concerned because with his experience of the Geneva Conventions, something that you've talked about, he knew it was a war crime, and he recalled a conversation in which he said to the warden of the Heliodrom, Stanko Bozic, that he should be careful because it was a war crime. With the suspicions that you had, what did you do, Dr. Bagaric?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to repeat. I was head of the Health Sector of the Croatian Defence Council, the Medical Sector, somebody who was in charge of that particular field. And relating to the organisation of the Health Service, I regularly received I don't know how many reports, but I never had reliable information about what you're asking me about until the people who were sent to perform certain jobs were wounded and then sent for treatment to the Mostar Hospital, and then all of those who had to be informed were informed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I'm going to ask you a technical question. In the Defence Department, headed by Mr. Stojic, because he was number one, would he summon meetings with several people to discuss questions? Would he summon you and other people to say, We have this and this problem. This is the situation. We have the Heliodrom. There are detainees. What do we do? Was this the way he worked, or was everything partitioned and you were not aware of the existence of a general policy, you would only take care of your 25 staff members, because you said there were 25 staff members, and there were no so-called thematic [Realtime transcript read in error "fanatic"] meetings or meetings on very significant issues? Could you tell us how this was organised? If Mr. Stojic were to testify, I'd ask the question directly, but for the time being I'm not aware at all of how this was organised. This is why I'm asking the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Just for the -- regarding the record, page 51, on line - what was it? - 22, an amusing misprint, because it said that there were no so-called fanatic meetings. "Thematic" was the word, not "fanatic." Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I talked about thematic meetings and not fanatic meetings. So, Witness, I'd like to thank my colleague for spotting the typo.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right. Your Honour, Mr. President, I'm talking about the time after my return from Canada. It was a time of open hostility and war, and at that time I really don't recall a single meeting that I attended. I don't think the collegium even met at that time, and quite honestly it was a time of great turmoil. Nobody knew what the next day would bring. People worked each in their own sector and did whatever they thought best. I, being in charge of my Health Sector, had my hands full, and I really don't recall any discussion on this topic in that period. And I don't think there were any thematic meetings at that time, or perhaps I didn't attend them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Did you at any stage raise with Mr. Stojic your concerns over whether there might be a forced labour programme at the Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let me go back to what I've just said. In a certain way, I focused and concentrated entirely on the health work, and I thought if the medical staff could help improve the situation, including on this point, I informed Mr. Stojic of that intention.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Well, for the people who were being injured and killed as a result of the Heliodrom labour programme that they were going to need medical help, but you were also a brigadier in the HVO, and it was that organisation that was using people from the Heliodrom to perform dangerous, life-threatening work. If you had suspicions about it, wouldn't it have been the most natural thing in the world for you to say to Bruno Stojic, You know, I'm not sure, but I think we might have a problem at the Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We all knew that we had a problem at the Heliodrom, in terms of all the aspects of the situation. I'm coming back to the part where you said that people got wounded, and to be honest, during the initial period --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: I wonder if you could just focus on forced labour and people being taken out of the Heliodrom to work, rather than telling us about all aspects of the situation, which you know is not what I'm asking you. Why don't you just try?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a physician, as the chief of the HVO Medical Corps, I did not have any reliable information to that effect. I never heard that something of the kind was happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: I wonder if you would look, please, at the document in the binder that you were given earlier today and you still have in front of you. It's P04352, and it's a letter dated the 20th of August of 1993, over the name of Stanko Bozic, and it's addressed to Bruno Stojic, and it's headed "Military Secret." And it's writing -- Stanko Bozic writing to Mr. Stojic to tell him that there's been a visit by the International Committee of the Red Cross, and can you see that the items that are said to be in violation of the Geneva Conventions within the Heliodrom are, number 1, "sending detainees to work," and then they go on to talk about food and bad conditions. I want to ask you --

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: -- from the other end now. Did Bruno Stojic ever say to you, Dr. Bagaric, you have people from your section going into the Heliodrom. Any information about sending detainees to work? Did he ever raise that topic with you?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, of course Bruno Stojic knew that our doctors did go to the Heliodrom, and if my colleague (redacted) -- I apologise. If my colleague said that -- I apologise. I believe that this has to be redacted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, this has to be redacted. Will you continue, please, Mr. Bagaric.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] During that period of time when he left, and later on when I left, of course that Bruno Stojic knew that, and it was our intention, in a certain way during those tortured and difficult times, to carry out a humanitarian intervention with a view to protecting health in the area. I believe that it was not just him who was well informed about the whole situation, that there were others.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: It may be just the interpretation, but I'm not clear -- genuinely not clear what you're saying there. In the English, it says: "During that period of time when he left, and later on when I left, of course that Bruno Stojic knew that, and it was our intention, in a certain way during those tortured and difficult times, to carry out a humanitarian intervention." Can you just answer the question for me? Are you saying that Bruno Stojic knew or did not know that there was a forced labour programme within the Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not say that, no. You asked me initially whether I informed Mr. Bruno Stojic -- this is your last question, whether I informed him that we, as physicians, when it came to the establishment of healthcare in the Heliodrom, and I said, in answer to that, that he must have known that. And now on to your question as to what Bruno Stojic knew, what he knew before the report on the 20th of August, I really don't know. I don't know that Bruno Stojic knew that people over there were forced to do physical labour. I don't know whether he knew that or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, Dr. Bagaric, you have here in front of you a letter, the letter which the director of the prison sent to Mr. Stojic. This letter is important because it reveals that Mr. Bozic has a warning about the future, has questions about the future, perhaps concerning this Tribunal, and he says, I don't want to be responsible or liable. Therefore, he concludes also by saying that all this must not in any way be reproached to the commander of the prison or the commander of the HVO, in the interests of "our people." Therefore, this is a very alarming letter, because it speaks of breaches of the Geneva Conventions, it says that there are detainees working outside. So a document as important as this one of the 20th of August, you never heard about it? You never heard anything about it, because a person who is responsible was actually thinking of the Tribunal and of the possibility of being indicted. You never heard about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I answered the Prosecutor's question and I said that I didn't know, and I didn't know whether Bruno Stojic was aware of that before the 20th of August. I was talking about that period of time. But it is clear that if Bruno Stojic received this paper, then on the 20th of August he became aware of that. But I was talking about the period before that period, so I'm not sure. There's no way for me to know what he knew about those things very specifically. I, as a doctor, subsequently learned that people were wounded when taken to do certain jobs, and I heard that as a doctor, looking after people in the hospital. I heard it in the hospital from people who were there after a certain period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Let's just turn the page with that document, if we may. Sorry, part of what I said was cut off there, and that's my fault. Can we just turn the page, and can you find the sentence that begins: "After the Red Cross's departure, we were not able to remedy these wrong-doings." Can you see those words? It's about six lines from the bottom of the letter. And the next sentence reads -- do you have that, Dr. Bagaric?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. Is this in Mr. Bozic's document? Just a moment. Please bear with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: "After the Red Cross's departure, we were not able to remedy these wrong-doings. On the contrary, the number of wounded and killed at the workplace is increasing by the day." So I'm going to come back to the question that I asked you a few moments ago. Did Mr. Stojic ever say to you, Well, Dr. Bagaric, you have people going into the Heliodrom. Can you help me with whether people are being wounded and killed? The people that you have going into the Heliodrom are doctors, who might well learn of things of that kind taking place. Did Mr. Stojic ever --

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Could the witness just answer the question, unless there's an objection to the form of the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I would object to the form of the question. The witness said if Bruno Stojic had received this letter. First of all, we should learn about what the witness knows about whether Bruno Stojic received the letter, and then we could proceed. In the transcript, just a moment, I'm going to draw attention to the correct page, it is page 56, line 9, the witness said, "if Bruno Stojic received this paper."

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: We don't have an opportunity to ask him, and I'm asking the witness whether Bruno Stojic ever raised with him the contents of it. That might help us on the issue of whether he received it, and it might be relevant to the case more generally. In my submission, it's a perfectly fair question which the witness can answer, if he chooses to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Did Stojic ever say to him, Anything from your inspections that can help me as to whether it's true that people were being killed and injured on forced labour at the Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said why my men went there, and I personally. And as for your specific question, what you're asking about, I don't remember. I don't remember that this ever transpired.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: The reason that your men went there is totally unconnected to the answer to my question, which is: Did Bruno Stojic ever raise it with you? It's not a hard question, Dr. Bagaric. You are, I respectfully suggest to you, capable of telling us whether the truth is that he did, or he didn't, or you can't remember.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I claim with full responsibility that I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: You don't know whether Mr. Stojic ever said to you, Just down the road, there's a place where I've heard people are being killed and injured? You just don't know whether that's the position?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that Bruno Stojic ever told me that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers please be asked not to overlap. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: The truth is, I'm going to suggest to you, that this was something that was not a secret to anyone. It was well known, and it was tolerated because it was useful. And that's the truth about this, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I said that this was a well-known matter. It was well known that people were taken for work. But I also said that I learned that only subsequently. I learned that from the professionals in the war hospital that I would encounter from time to time who would tell me about people having been treated there. I said clearly that I don't remember that Bruno Stojic ever said to me, Go there because people are being wounded over there. I repeat, I was in charge of the Healthcare Service, which means that if people were anywhere, working or soldiering, of any ethnic affiliation, we intervened, as physicians, as the Health Service, so it would have been totally superfluous for him to tell me, Somebody has been wounded, you have to go and assist them. That would have been unnecessary, and that's what I said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your answer enables me to continue on a matter. Just let's take an assumption, a concrete case, so that everybody can understand the problem. Imagine a case of a prisoner who is doing a certain job or work. I don't qualify it as forced labour. He goes from the prison, outside the prison, to do a job, and then he is injured by a bullet and he is taken to the military hospital where he is going to be immediately treated by a doctor. If, for instance, he's received a bullet in his lung, the bullet is going to be extracted and so on. We know, because we've been in this case for years and we know all the details, we know that normally when somebody is admitted in hospital, there is the name on the book, the register, the date of his entry, the first diagnosis which is made, for instance, wound to the chest by a bullet, and then there is also who the person is, a soldier, civilian, prisoner. Normally, one will indicate "prisoner." The doctor, the surgeon who is going to operate upon him and extract the bullet automatically knows that it is a prisoner who has been injured by a bullet outside the prison. This information -- this doctor, shouldn't he convey this by the chain of command to say that he, as a doctor, he has operated upon a prisoner who normally was supposed to be in a prison and not receive a bullet outside of the prison, or be hit? If there is a report of this type, did you have any knowledge of that, yourself, because there hasn't been only one person injured, there have been several persons injured and there have been several people killed? So this is a -- have you seen or heard any sort of report of this kind which would have come to you through medical channels?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand your question. The war hospital in Mostar, which was in the very centre of the city and which treated the wounded, any wounded, all wounded, I believe that at that moment the physicians who treated a patient didn't know the circumstances of their wounding. There were -- was a lot of wounded, different pathology. I spent most of the time in Mostar or in the field all over the place. My office was in Mostar. However, during that period of time I don't remember ever having received a report speaking of somebody who was wounded while performing certain work. It was only later on when I read some reports, but that was much later. The reports were issued by our physicians who went there, and I learned from the reports that such wounding did happen, but it was a time when it was a notorious fact that things like that could have happened. However, I don't want to dwell upon the circumstances. I'm not questioning how things happened. Somebody could have been working within the camp and still be wounded because it was all a war zone, or maybe they could have been taken to the front-line to work, I don't know, on the protection of what shall I call those lines and be wounded like that, but that was only later, subsequently. Such cases, I believe -- I don't believe that they were that frequent, but it was later on when everybody was in a position to learn about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Would you have a look, please, at document P05465. P05465, a little further on in your binder.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Yeah, I saw it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Thank you. This is a document dated the 29th of September of 1993. Again, it's over the name of Stanko Bozic. This time it appears to be directed to you, Dr. Bagaric. Can you see your name there?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can see my name, yes, and this does refer to me, if the document was sent directly to me. Actually, this document was sent directly to me. However, I had already seen the document in my first testimony. I don't remember this document precisely, but I know exactly what it is and how it was, and I am willing to comment upon it, Your Honour. I'm willing to comment upon it, because I believe it's very important.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Doctor, Stanko Bozic has some concerns. In particular, he tells you that there are difficulties and problems encountered regarding the treatment of some severely wounded and sick inmates, due to inadequate accommodation, insufficient material and medicaments. And he wants you to arrange the transfer of sick people, and he points out that there's to be a visit by the Red Cross, and that's another good reason to move those who are sick out of prison and into a hospital. All right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can read it in the document, exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: How did you think, when you got that letter, that people in a prison might be severely wounded?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said that this was on the 29th of September. I'm talking about the 29th of September. I remember this document from the previous case, where -- during which I testified. I beg your pardon. No, this is very important, the date is very important, because when we are talking about the month of June, Your Honour, it's not the same. It's not the same, whether it is June, July. This was a time of chaos, this was also a chaotic time. However, a bit later and before this document was issued, we had already carried out various interventions. The Prosecutor, I am not going to say that he did it intentionally. I understand that he wants to state his case and tries to discredit me as a witness, but I believe that you should know that before this document was issued --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Dr. Bagaric, as a witness, first of all, let me again ask you what I have done already before, that you should speak slowly and to wait a bit after questions, et cetera. But my second and probably equally important remark is that you should not, in a way, criticise the Prosecutor. He's doing his job. You have to answer the question. If you are not satisfied with the form of the question, then of course you may mention this, and then the Chamber is going to take a decision about it. But again I say that, as usual, you have been speaking quite, in a way, as an extended way, but please try to concentrate on the question itself. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Prandler.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: The question was this: How did you think, when you got that letter, that people in a prison might be severely wounded?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never said that I had received this letter. I never claimed that I remember this letter. I remember this letter from the previous case in which I testified. At that time, I objected to this letter, although I respect Mr. Bozic, and I would like to express my respect for the way he looked after the people at a very difficult time. However, what I'm saying is -- is that it is very important, and it doesn't matter whether I see the letter or not. What matters is that two very important documents have been skipped here, and they were all issued in August. Before this letter, we had already done a lot in providing health service at the Heliodrom. There are two documents -- I will go back to your question. I understand. I'm coming back to your question. I apologise, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Mr. President, to just confine ourselves to this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Dr. Bagaric, the Prosecutor is asking you questions about a document, and I want to be fair. I'm not taking sides. I just see that when you received this document, you couldn't infer that these people had been wounded outside the prison, because there is nothing said about forced labour in the document. Simply, the director of the prison calls your attention on the fact that some detainees are wounded and have to be treated, and strangely, curiously, at the one-but-last paragraph, he uses nearly the same words as those used in the letter of the 20th of August, and between the letter and this, there have been exactly 148 other documents from the prison. This is number 722, and in August 574, so there were 148. And despite the time span during several weeks of 148 documents, he literally lifts this same wording of his preceding letter, and he doesn't speak of the Tribunal and he doesn't speak of forced labour, but he underscores the question of the health situation of wounded detainees and asks you to take the necessary steps. So the Prosecutor was asking you, Have you been aware of this document, have you known about this document, and you have answered this document was already talked about during another testimony. And what we are interested to know is whether, on the 29th of -- you had in your office this document in front of you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the 29th of September, not the 29th of August. You mean the 29th of September, don't you, 29th of September? I don't remember this document. However -- however, if you will allow me, I would still like to say a sentence that I believe is very important. My colleague, whom I mentioned very often here, (redacted) (redacted) was a much more relevant source of information than Mr. Bozic, when it came to treatment, medical care, the supplies of medicines and medical supplies. Even before this date, we had already carried out a forceful humanitarian intervention in order to provide everything that Mr. Bozic is complaining about in this letter. Even before that, we transferred the sick and probably the wounded. A relationship was already established between the prison and the hospital in Mostar. It was already well known who was doing what already at that time. So if I received reports from (redacted) that a medical point had been established there, that people were being examined and treated, that doctors were engaged there, and I myself issued an order that this is how things should be done and implemented, then I believe (redacted) and my colleagues. I personally was not very concerned and worried by this report, as regards the healthcare, because I knew that it was being applied and it was under full control, very firm control.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, one has to redact the name of the doctor which features several times on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: As I understand it, you're saying you're not sure whether you got it, and we appreciate that. Could you look, please, at the words that are three lines above the entry enclosure, the list of the wounded and sick. You can see a sentence which reads as follows: "I kindly ask you again to use your influence to have this issue solved." Dr. Bagaric, there isn't, with respect to you, I'm going to suggest, any getting away from it. Stanko Bozic was telling you, in this letter and on other occasions, that people in the Heliodrom were wounded, needed medical attention, and the question that I asked you I don't know how long ago is one that, in the circumstances, I'm going to ask for your help with again. Can you help us whether you knew, now, having looked at that, and the word "again," can you help us with whether you knew --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to intervene, because the question of the Prosecution is formed in such a way that, from a medical point of view, you might be mistaken. We all have this letter in front of us. This letter distinguishes between two categories, the wounded detainees and the sick detainees, and contrary with what the Prosecutor says in the sentence he quoted, it's only about the sick, not the wounded. So medically speaking, can one infer this: The wounded people have been treated properly and put back in prison under medical help, but for the sick people, no, you don't know what illness, when you see this letter perhaps you don't have the medicines or the equipment, and he requests they're -- that they are admitted in hospital, because they already come from the hospital? So if they come from the hospital, it's not necessary to send them back to the hospital. But for the sick, maybe they need to be admitted in the hospital, so shouldn't there be here a medical reading of this letter? While the Prosecutor seems to take the two aspects together, that is to say, the wounded and the sick, my impression in this letter, that is, the wounded treated in the hospital, it is not necessary to send them back to hospital, while the sick, yes, it is necessary. Could you interpret or read this letter in this way or the way the Prosecution reads it? I'm asking the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. To your question, which is absolutely correct, I would like to provide a very concise answer. Mr. Bozic says here, when it comes to the treatment of a certain number of seriously sick and wounded persons who have been brought in, due to the inadequate conditions of accommodation and the lack of medicines and medical supplies, during that period of time, and I'm saying this before you, Your Honours, at that time in the centre, we provided not only a medical point, but even beds. I'm not actually sure about that. However, we had a medical point. I don't know whether this was in this particular period of time, but I believe so. I'm not sure. I believe that we even had accommodation for our doctors who were detainees. That's one thing. And then, secondly, when it says "move the sick and provide them with hospital care," that was a common occurrence. Very often, doctors, detainees, Muslims, would very often determine who among the detainees could not be treated in the prison but rather in the hospital, and whenever that happened, whenever they requested that, those people would be sent for treatment to the hospital, and I'm claiming that with full responsibility here. Sometimes they may have been delayed, due to the overall situation. However, eventually they would be sent to the hospital. I remember that I intervened several times, not many times, maybe a couple of times, when they could not deal with that at the level of the hospital and the prison. On the other hand, when he's talking here about again using your influence, I would like to explain and say that this was absolutely as I'm going to tell you. If I had received this letter from Bozic, this could have been only the first letter from him, not the second. Why is that? Because he says here this is in the spirit of the Croatian language, and that was something that we often used -- I use it myself often whenever I write a letter to somebody. In the first part of the letter, he says, I'm sending you this letter to inform you about this and that and the other and so on and so forth, and then he continues to say this and he finishes by saying, I am addressing you again, which means for the second time in the same letter, not in the second letter. Sir, I am convinced that this was the first letter -- if I ever received it, that this was the first letter from Bozic, I'm convinced, and that the second part or the latter part of the letter actually follows up on the first part of the letter. This -- soon after that we intervened in order to see what was actually going on there, although I'm not even sure that we ever received this letter, or maybe that intervention of ours coincided with the letter. I really don't know, but there are other documents that can confirm what I have just told you. I remember that intervention of ours, but I don't remember this particular letter, not at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Turn over, please, to P05503, which is a letter written by a commission that includes 2D-AB. And we can see on page 3 of the English that it is addressed both to you personally and to Bruno Stojic, and I think in one of your earlier answers you were saying, Well, compared to Stanko Bozic, I'd rather have the information from 2D-AB. And here, sir, you have it under the heading "Proposed Measures." At item 4, it is proposed by the commission that the seriously ill and wounded should be transferred to the Mostar HVO War Hospital. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it. It's a very important document. I can see it. May I answer this? This is not a letter from some commission. This is the letter from the commission of the most reliable people for whom I am a superior; Dr. Sandrk, Dr. Curic, et cetera. If you compare this to the previous letter, where Mr. Bozic writes that he is dissatisfied because there is a lack of medicines, and he wrote that letter on the 29th September, if we look at this letter carefully, it is possible that this intervention of ours coincided by chance. But it says the infirmary of the centre is well supplied with medicines and medical supplies. I'm sorry, but I really believed Sandrk, Kolak and Curic more than anyone else. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, I waited for the witness to finish his answer. I have a technical objection. I already informed the Prosecution and I said that there is a mistake in the translation of the stamp, and I expected this error would be corrected, but I can see again that the wrong translation of the stamp is being used again. It's the stamp on the first page of the document. In the English version, it says that it is the Department of the Defence, and below that the Administration of Military Police. And in the original, we see that it's the Defence Department; no mention of the military police. I was told before that it would be corrected. I'm talking about the front page.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Well, I will certainly see to it that that stamp is investigated. Can we just stick with the issue of people who are seriously ill and wounded and who need to be transferred to hospital.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I did not understand, the question has not been asked, but in order to concentrate and for the sake of time, I really think the witness should be allowed to finish and tell us who was attending during this meeting. The previous document was of the 29th. The current one is the 30th. The information contained is different. If this is not done, I will do it in re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: No, I'm sorry. I'm going to have to object to that objection. The witness was asked a very specific question about item number 4, and he started by telling us about the composition of the commission, and then went on to talk about the infirmary. It's a question that can be dealt with very easily.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: We can see in this letter, this report, Dr. Bagaric, coming to you, that your colleague, whose word you esteem, is reporting to you that there are seriously ill and wounded people within the Heliodrom, and I'm going to come back to the question that I asked you a while ago. When you got that report, did you think to yourself, How are people being wounded in the Heliodrom? This isn't people whose wounds have been treated in hospital and have come back to the Heliodrom. This is people who need to go to hospital. Weren't you concerned to know what they were doing there?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: I would appreciate it if the witness could answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours -- I'm sorry? Right, no problem. I would just like to ask the Prosecutor where he sees, in point 4, that these people were wounded in Heliodrom. Where can we see that in point 4? I just want to say that something is implied in the question that is not there in point 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: It's completely beside the point. These people need to be transferred to hospital from prison. Whether they were wounded in the prison, outside the prison, they are people who need hospital treatment for their wounds. They are in prison. I suspect we all agree that they should not be in prison. The witness was receiving information to that effect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Prosecutor, in paragraph 4 it is said that the seriously ill and wounded should be transferred to the Mostar Hospital. This is all it says. Well, one may think that the wounded were wounded when working outside the camp, but possibly.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Absolutely. I'm not saying that it says that for a moment. What I'm saying is, when this witness received this information, did it not occur to him to wonder why people were being wounded whilst they were in the Heliodrom or wounded and then being taken to the Heliodrom rather than to hospital? It's a fair question. He's come to tell us that, in his opinion, the medical care was very good. These documents, we suggest, show the contrary. And I can be allowed to ask him that question, in my submission, and I would appreciate an answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Doctor, can you answer the Prosecution's question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can't see anything from this. I quite agree with what you said, Your Honour, but I'm here for the Defence, but more than anything I am here for you, so that you are able to take the right decision sometime in the future. On this document, I was trying to show certain things that really need to be understood, and it's difficult to understand them without taking into account the whole situation that preceded this. It's very important to note that at one of the collegium meetings in that month, we discussed -- and this is the only meeting I remember discussing the topic of Heliodrom, and until then we physicians had already intervened, and we were a constant presence there. This is, in fact, proof, Your Honour, that we continually, constantly monitored the situation, except for Dr. Curic, who was there. And in addition to the medical point that was organised there, in addition to all that, I sent those three physicians, and they were not sending me this report as to a stranger. They know very well who sent them there. I sent them as a follow-up of our constant monitoring. And you see here below it says: "Enclosed, command of the Health Centre of the 8th of September, 1993." That is two days prior. That command, that order, is an order that I personally signed. So they offer here a very important instruction, how to proceed. They appraise everyone of the problem. They send it to the office of the president, the Defence Department, the Main Staff, the Health Sector. Why did they write "Health Sector"? Because I sent them. The Office for Exchange, et cetera, and even the director of the centre. They say that he was there together with them during the inspection. And Dr. Pehar was there, who was outside the brigade, and the other doctor who was working at the infirmary. So at that time we had continuous supervision at Heliodrom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Doctor, we have this document saying that three doctors -- three doctors draft a report, and in item 5 state that the seriously ill and wounded must be transferred to the war hospital. Say I'm Mr. Mate Boban, I receive that report, because that's sent to him, and I see item 4 and, okay, think, Well, this is Mr. Bagaric's responsibility because he's a doctor. I'm Mr. Stojic, I receive that letter, I look at item 4, and I say, well, this is a medical question which is the responsibility of the Medical Sector, so this is what I think. What do you think of that? I'm Mr. Tole from headquarters, I can see it's medical, This is not my area of my competence, it is the area of Dr. Bagaric. So you're on the front-line there, and this is what the Prosecution wants to ascertain. What did you do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely, we complied with this. I don't remember specifically a specific document so as to be able to show you, but I claim with full responsibility that within a day or two this problem was solved. My commission and my people said that this needed to be done, but not only that. They wrote many things with a view to improving the health situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Dr. Bagaric, you're here as a witness, and your task is to answer questions. Do you remember what the question is here? The question is: Did you inquire -- did you wonder how come there are these people wounded in Heliodrom? Why were they wounded? That is the question. You talk at length around and beside, but you do not answer the question. So would you please be so kind and to limit yourself to precisely answer the question which is asked of you, full stop. When the Prosecutor wants more comment, he asks you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Trechsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Dr. Bagaric, you've just finished telling us that you would have acted on this within a day or two and the problem would have been solved. Would you turn, please, to document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm a bit astonished, Mr. Laws. You asked the question many lines ago. Now I ask the witness to answer the question, and instead of letting him answer --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: -- or wait whether he does, you go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: I thought -- Judge Trechsel, I do apologise. I thought you were giving him an instruction for the future, and I'm turning to the next document in the sequence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Well, the question is still unanswered.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: The question is still unanswered, I agree, and if the witness would like to answer it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: -- he of course may.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I should -- I mean, I want to answer. It was a time where wounding was such a frequent occurrence in all parts of town. Wounding, as wounding, did not cause surprise, or wonderment, so on the 30th of September it was abundantly clear to everyone that prisoners are used from time to time. I think that everyone knew that prisoners performed certain jobs around the detention centre, that shells were falling around, that people were exposed to risk and got wounded. What was more important to me was to assess the situation and redress irregularities than to go into the nature of disease and wounding. The medical approach was more important.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you turn then, please, to document P502 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Hold on. Witness, there is something important in this document, item 7, because obviously the members of the commission wanted to place you under supervision, because look at item number 7. They state that the Department of Defence had to be informed of measures to be taken by the 1st of October at noon, and then they add the reference to the fax number. So it is that commission's view that there is an emergency and that action needs to be taken. And earlier on, you said, Well, I did act, because everything was settled, and this is important. Do you confirm that you have taken all the necessary steps to implement this commission's recommendations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Under item 7, we have the telephone number at my office. It's my office. We didn't leave this item 7 and send it to the office of Mate Boban so that he reply. We wanted to appraise him of the problem, and everyone was to address problems at their level. So with regard to the health situation, of course that care existed. We got information, what was done and how much progress was made, and we constantly monitored that situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But, Doctor, by this answer do you mean to say that it was up to Mr. Boban to give the green light, because we are talking about medical issues?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know that. We didn't ask him whether -- to intervene or not, medically. We wouldn't have asked him, ever. We intervened without anyone's permission because it was a priority, and this order wasn't created in agreement with Boban.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Your Honour, if you allow me. Perhaps the translation of item 7 is wrong that appears from your question, because in item 7 it says: "Inform the Defence Department on the aforementioned measures." That's the telephone number for reporting on the measures taken. We got translation from French that you asked, Were you informed of these measures? On the contrary, this point provides the possibility for others to inform the Defence Department.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that was our telephone to which people could report on the measures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Doctor, listening to you, the doctor drafting the report suggests measures, and he's the one to implement those?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. He is the one who would supervise their actions, their implementation. It doesn't depend on us at the Health Sector. It depends on the doctor in the 3rd Brigade. It depends -- it says, look, that the centre is in a very bad state. How is it possible for prisoners to be used for labour, whereas the centre itself is not clean and tidy? We came to the centre, and we put the health situation of the people there under constant supervision, and to the best of our abilities, we were rather successful. For that part, I am really prepared to take all responsibility that it was indeed as I described.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we turn to document P05812. P05812. It's a letter dated the 11th of October of 1993 to Bruno Stojic, and I would ask you, please, to find the paragraph numbered 2. You'll see that at the foot of the letter, it's over the name of Stanko Bozic. Can you find paragraph 2, Doctor?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so. Please quote. I think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: It says that there's severe wounding and other suffering of the detainees: "A. A large number of wounded detainees need the kind of medical attention that can only be administered at hospital, which we are unable to provide." Then it goes on to deal again with the problem of supply of medical equipment and so forth. Can we try to take this one quite shortly? You agree with me that if Stanko Bozic is right, then the problem of people with wounds who need hospitalisation is continuing?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Speaking of this segment of health security, of course the situation was not ideal either there or in Mostar, certainly not. Mr. Bozic is not right when he speaks of the Health Sector, with two doctors at the centre, plus extra doctors from outside who report to us at the same time and say that from the point of view of health support and health protection, the situation is quite satisfactory. Of course, in other circumstances it would not have been satisfactory, but for that situation that prevailed there, it was different. Our representative talked tete-a-tete with the doctors who worked there, and then in cooperation with our physicians they kept improving and improving the measures. There was always room for improvement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Laws, I would like to ask a question about this very paragraph issue refers to. That is on the English text, of course, page 2, paragraph 2, and I don't know why, but there are two As there, and the second one I am referring to, and there is a remark. And I would like to ask the witness to concentrate on that remark, and it is being stated, and I quote: "The International Committee of the Red Cross visited the SVZ on the 10th, 11th and 12th August 1993 and pointed out a number of irregularities that also constitute violations of the Geneva Conventions." And here is the first item, sub-point A, which says that: "The use of detainees for work." We have already -- end of quotation. We have already talked about the possibility -- rather, we talked about the very fact that there were wounded detainees there, but of course it was not clear what was the causes of their wounds, et cetera. Now, I wonder if you have -- this report was, of course, sent to you, and -- rather, to Mr. Bruno Stojic, but you received it as well, and I wonder if you have not looked at it at that time and if you had -- if you had done anything to, in a way, to see to it that the detainees should not be used for work. It is my question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, Your Honour, but I have here a document that was sent to Bruno Stojic. That's what's written here. And the next document that you're probably referring to begins with item 2, but it has no heading. Is that the same document, or perhaps the pages are not properly organised in my version? They must be. Just a minute. In my version, I have 1, then 6 and 7 and 8. That's what confused me. The last page should be -- should come last, and in my version it's in the middle. That's what confused me. So this document was received by Bruno Stojic and Zarko Tole. This is the 11th of October, a long time after the setting up of that centre for isolation or prison. So if this indeed happened as Stanko Bozic is saying, then all those who should have known about it certainly knew. I'm trying to say that my job, as a doctor, was first of all to organise health protection inside, and that people who needed medical assistance should be brought to the hospital. And I guarantee here that it all functioned well even when I was not there, because everyone had their very clear assignment. But, of course, I don't remember who was wounded, how, and what kind of injuries they had, but I say with full responsibility that under the circumstances, we created excellent conditions for medical staff. Once, I spoke to one of the detainees, who was a physician himself, who told me openly, We did a great job, and he was referring to me and himself and all those who were there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Thank you. Dr. Bagaric, at the same time I would like to refer back to an earlier document which we have seen and which was addressed to you by Mr. Bozic, and in that he makes reference to the impending visit of the ICRC delegation, and therefore he asks you, and of course other colleagues, to do something with the wounded. So these two documents are very much interrelated, and that is why I asked you this question. I am not quite convinced that you have, in a way, taken care at that time about the -- I mean, not personally you, but I mean your service, if you had done the necessary actions and took the necessary actions either to take care of the wounded, but of course I also took note of your answer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm sorry. Before we get too far ahead, I just want to say that not the entire answer of the witness is recorded. On page 79, he said the document is addressed to Bruno Stojic, if he ever received it. It's very important to me, and it's not on the record.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I need, if you allow me to, to provide a clarification with regard to what the honourable Judge said, for the sake of the full truth. The first letter by Bruno Stojic on the 29th September, where he says there is not enough medicine, and on the 30th of September our commission goes out and, together with him, inspects the situation, and they say that the supply of medicines is quite adequate, so it looks -- this looks to me like a standard form letter. There is a shortage of medicine, there is no shortage of medicine, et cetera. I appreciate his concern, but, Your Honours, it was more important to me what physicians have to say about that. And, second, the first thing was written on the 29th September and the second thing on the 11th of October, quite a while after. By that time, every sick person and every wounded person was transferred for proper treatment. I don't know if there were any more woundings after that, but if there were, we intervened; if not me, personally, those who had the assignment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We're going to take a break for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Prosecutor, Mr. Laws, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Dr. Bagaric, I'm going to ask you a few very short questions, and can we try and make a little progress with "yes" or "no." They're going to be very easy. Is it right that you never went to the Dretelj prison?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it right that you never went to Gabela?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never, it is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: And it's the same answer for Ljubuski?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Same answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: But your colleague, Dr. 2-AB [sic], was going to each of those facilities, was he not?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is in line with what I was already talking about. We were continuously monitoring what was happening in the detention centres and prisons, and so on and so forth. We engaged local physicians from the local units regularly and continuously. Within the detention centres, we formed the points which employed detainees doctors, (redacted) (redacted), was in charge of the coordination of all these tasks, and I regularly received his reports and together talked with him I talked about that, and that's why I didn't go there myself. And the gentleman whom you mentioned, he did, because that's -- that was part of our agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Yes. And he was going there in his capacity as a member of your staff, your subordinate, to write reports which came to you and to the Health Sector; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is true that he submitted reports and he sent them to several addresses. Based on his reports, I also issued certain commands and orders with regard to the improvements that he thought were necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Would you turn, please, to document P04756?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] No, I cannot find. [Interpretation] I apologise to the Trial Chamber. Can I say one thing that is very important? I omitted saying this before, and this is the last time I'm asking you for such thing. I've noticed something very important that I would like to deal with, and it refers to the previous document dated 11 October 1993, issued by Mr. Bozic. Mr. Bozic writes about something based on which the Judge could conclude that nothing had been undertaken. However, I adhere by my previous words and I continue repeating that we continuously monitored the situation. However, in item 2, Bozic himself says what the Committee of the Red Cross on the 10th/11th of December saw and what they pointed out. It says "taking prisoners to work." Secondly, the quality and quantity of food and improvements. Number 3, bad conditions in solitary cells. None of the three things fall within the purview of the healthcare sector or the doctors that were in charge of implementing that. This is very important and it should be recorded. He is talking about the healthcare situation, I understand his concern. However, this report issued by the Red Cross confirms that what he's talking about, from the medical point of view, was not the way he describes it. And I would like to finish with that, and I apologise for this intervention. So we are talking about his document, that document that we discussed previously. I'd like to thank you. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much for these specifications.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Well, since you raise it, Dr. Bagaric, of course it was not your role to feed the detainees within the HVO prisons, but your section learnt that they were being inadequately fed and that they were becoming malnourished as a result, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were such problems, and it is true that an order was issued to remove that problem. This is not a direct healthcare issue, but it could have an impact on health, and this was sent to the warden, to the doctors who were there, and to all the others who were in charge of that issue. This was a direct recommendation by our commission to do that, and according to what I know and the subsequent reports, you can see that the situation with that regard considerably improved at the Heliodrom. There was still certain problems every now and then, but generally speaking, that problem was being dealt with and finally became rather satisfactory.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: We spent quite a lot of time with your colleague 2D-AB on the topic of nourishment. The position in other centres, do you agree with me, was simply appalling? We can take it as quickly as that, can't we ?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to his reports, I can't say that the situation was appalling, but it was not satisfactory. Every now and then, it was not satisfactory and efforts were made to remove all the problems, to point to the problem and help with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: I don't want to do the same exercise as I did before, but not satisfactory is one thing. People were reduced to shocking physical states as a result of their detention by the HVO. That's what it comes down to, isn't it? You know that, don't you, Doctor?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that some people were indeed quite malnourished.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: And so if we look, please, at document P04756 --

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please repeat the number. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: I think we turned it up just a few moments ago. It should be the one open in front of you. These are the minutes --

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Yeah, okay, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: These are the minutes of the heads of the Defence Department held on the 2nd of September, 1993, and Bruno Stojic was there. And if we turn to see item 4, we can see that you were there?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was at the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: And I think you looked at this briefly when Ms. Nozica was asking you questions. Under item 3, and it's page 4 of the English and it's page 3 in the B/C/S, we have an entry: "Military prisons are another example of very bad work. The head took the floor and said ..." Can you see those words?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please continue. I'm looking, and I'm sure I'll find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: You're looking, good. "My opinion is that we have two military prisons." Can you see those words?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm listening. Go on, go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: "Heliodrom -- Heliodrom and the military prison Ljubuski. As for the other places where detainees are held, Gabela and Dretelj, I do not consider them as military facilities and refuse to personally endorse the work of these institutions." Can you see those words?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: But your colleague, Witness 2D-AB, had been inspecting those facilities as your subordinate as a member of the Department of Defence, hadn't he?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, a member of the Health Sector of the Defence Department.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: So did it not strike you as odd in that meeting that the head of that department was saying, actually, that they weren't his responsibility?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I have to elaborate. I won't be long, I promise. I see that your time is very precious. I remember that meeting. That was the first time that I heard of the form of something being military or non-military. This follows up on my yesterday's words, when I said that I didn't know whether something was a detainee centre, a central prison, an isolation centre or whatever. It was at that time that I was able to make a distinction between a central prison in Ljubuski, and in that case the head had in mind the Defence Department that he was in charge with, and he was talking about his responsibility, or the responsibility of the Defence Department. And as for the other centres, he believed that he -- or he actually didn't know what that was all about, he didn't know who was behind them, and so on and so forth. However, Your Honours, I, as a physician, and I'm talking from that point of view, I really did not care and it didn't make any difference as to who had established any of them. I don't know whether there are any documents signed by anybody about their establishment. What mattered to us was to be present there all the time in order to improve the healthcare and the condition of health. Two months before this meeting, until the end of the year, you will find all the 20 documents talking about efforts that were made in order to improve the situation. When Mr. Stojic says that he does not deny their existence, he's talking more about the formal responsibility, who should be formally in charge of each of them, and that's how I personally understood his words. That's what I believed at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Well, who was going to be in charge of them if not him?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Honestly, I don't know, especially from the position of the times which were as they were. And all the time as we're talking about that, you have to bear that in mind that the situation was really difficult, and I claim with full responsibility that nobody could control the overall situation. I personally, when I said that it was not the Defence Department, I said that yesterday or the day before yesterday, what I meant, I was talking within the context of never having heard that a decision of that sort or -- was either made or signed by the Defence Department. I never saw such a decision. Nobody put me abreast of any such decision. Nobody ever asked for my opinion. Given the area of responsibility of certain units and the doctors who, in one way or another, looked after the healthcare needs, there we established our contacts with them and the detained doctors. I personally issued an order to establish points later on, and before that, the supervision was constant. And this is all I know about the responsibility, and which detention centres belonged to whom and who was responsible, and when I say "responsible," I mean in charge of.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Just the previous month, your colleague 2D-AB had been in Dretelj, and now the person who's the head of his department is saying he doesn't endorse that facility. Didn't it at the time strike you as odd, as unusual, 2D-AB had been working on behalf of the department?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this point I'm going to object. First, it's been asked and answered. He's already indicated that as a physician, he did not hear as far as who was responsible for the facilities. As a physician, he cared for the individuals. So I think the question has been asked and answered.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Well, if I may reply, this witness's view, as a physician, is not really the question. The question is: What did he think when Stojic said it was nothing to do with him?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: He's already asked and answered that question as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Well, he hasn't answered it in a way that is remotely satisfactory. He's talked about a large number of other details and not answered that question. It's a straightforward question. He hasn't answered it at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, I leave it for the Trial Chamber to decide. But as far as I understand, he answered to the best of his ability. Whether it's satisfactory to the Prosecution or not, that's another question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are right, Mr. Karnavas, this is another matter. Mr. Laws, you can continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I just wish to say that I do not agree with this decision. I think the Prosecutor would have been right to go on. But I guess that I'm in a minority, but just for the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, not at all. There must be a mistake between Judges. We are not forbidding the Prosecution to continue. If he wanted to insist on the problem, he may continue. I didn't say the opposite. On the other hand, I just wanted to hasten on what Mr. Karnavas had said. You may continue, Mr. Laws.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Cast your mind back, Dr. Bagaric. You're in a meeting with the head of your department, and he's saying, Those prisons aren't anything to do with me. Didn't it strike you as odd that the same department had been inspecting them? That's the question that I've asked. Could you try to answer it, please?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely, absolutely. At that meeting, I didn't find anything strange. Personally, it really didn't matter to me who was responsible for what centre. I knew, even at that time when we were at that meeting, Your Honours, that our doctors and me personally, although I was not directly responsible, it was not my direct responsibility; however, I knew that we had undertaken all the measures that I've already spoken about at great length. I personally issued orders to do this, that, or the other. The gist of that was a continuous healthcare and surveillance, and my -- the person in charge was my colleague, and you know who it was. And now the answer to your question, how did he go there. He was in charge of preventive medicine in the Service for Hygiene and Epidemiology in all the units of the Croatian Defence Council. All the facilities which were in the areas of responsibility of these units were also his responsibility. For example, he would go and inspect the brigade, and he would also inspect, for example, a refugee centre which was within that brigade, or a detention centre. And together with his colleagues, doctors, he regularly controlled the healthcare situation there. That would be my answer to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Very well. Can we turn to the topic, please, of humanitarian aid, about which you spoke at some length yesterday and the day before, and I want to understand what your position is. You're here saying that you helped East Mostar with medicine and with supplies?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I said so, whenever I could, and even if I could do more, I would have. I'm very sad and I'm very hurt that my proposal that I tendered was not adopted, because there would be less war and less evil if it had been adopted. If the hospital in the centre of town could have been used as a joint hospital, that would have put an end to the war in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: You blame the international organisations for not doing enough to help?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't blame them. I am grateful to them. We had a little celebration of three years of war healthcare after the war, and I officially recognised their efforts. They are the people who had left their homes in Europe and came to our city in war to help us, and whatever they did, I will be eternally grateful to them. However, I believe that some of those organisations could have been much more efficient. This is my experience, and I would like somebody to look at that and to see how humanitarian work could be improved in the future. This is what I was talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: The word that you used was "disappointed" in them, in the international organisations?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I may have been disappointed every now and then, but now I've told you something that I believe is the closest to the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: And you also added, and it's the transcript page 82 of that day's evidence, that the Muslims didn't want to cooperate because they would not have been able to enjoy the reputation of victims. Do you recall saying that?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know what you're talking about, but this is not what I said. I said that I was always wondering how come there was no reply from the other side. When I asked UNPROFOR and the International Red Cross and the international representatives whether we were going to do something, for example, when I met as the person number one -- I am sorry to be sidetracking here, and I say with full responsibility that I offered very many times to meet to -- with the person number one on the other side, and this never materialised, and I wondered why that was. And I assumed that the doctors of the BH Army were not the ones who blocked those talks. I believe that it was somebody else. A politician very high up above them made those decisions and told them that they couldn't do that, because if you do that, then Croats will not be as evil as they wanted us to be at the time, because that was the message that they wanted to send to the world about the Croats in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and it is so clear. Your Honours, to this very day, Croats are -- do not enjoy a satisfying situation. During the war, Croats were halved in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and still there is no political solution to that problem. And if we were an animal species that was halved, I believe that we would --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Well, I am going to have to stop you there, Dr. Bagaric. You're now telling us about the reduction in Croat --

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: -- population, and I'm asking you about something that you said and asking you to confirm that part of the blame for what happened in East Mostar must be placed at the door of the Muslims, themselves. And, in essence, that is what you're saying, is it not?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not what I said. At least that's not how I said it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Well, what part of it have I misunderstood? A politician --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That's my whole point, Your Honour. He's misstating the record. He talked about they were getting orders from the higher up, so he's blaming higher political officials.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So if he's going to say Muslims, which we're talking everybody. It's like saying Croats or Serbs or whatever. You know, there's a big difference between the people and some high-level officials that are calling the shots. So if he wants to be precise and if he wants to get a precise answer from the gentleman, and not make him appear as if he's trying to be evasive, which seems to be part of the tactic here, then I suggest that he asks precise questions. I know the tactic, Your Honours. This is what happens: The witness doesn't want to answer because he sees Muslims in the general. He's talked about political authorities at the very top. So I would kindly ask for the Trial Chamber to direct the Prosecutor to be precise when quoting what the witness has stated. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct, yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, in your previous answer, was it an accurate, specific answer, or does it need to be complemented because Mr. Karnavas has taken the floor? Had you fully answered the Prosecution's question or did you want to qualify and to add things to your answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think counsel interpreted my position correctly. I think that's the problem, that's where the problem lies. I cannot blame the Muslims. I'm blaming the leadership, which was making political decisions at the time, decisions that were affecting people on the ground, the Croats and Muslims at war. That's what I meant, and that's why, when the Prosecutor asked the question the way he did, I said I believed it was not entirely true.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Let me try and phrase it in a way that you'll agree with.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Are you saying that somebody with political influence over the people living in East Mostar, somebody in that position was trying to bring about a situation where the people in East Mostar would not be helped? Is that the effect of it?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
