utterances.text: If one side of Mostar is suffering, both sides are affected, but one is affected more. We were faring better on the east than the other side. If one side has all the possibilities to resolve the problem of the other side, and the other side is not responding, I said I held that someone up there on the political level must have decided that this should not be done. That's what I meant, and I have nothing to add.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm going to explore with you, in the course of the rest of today and into tomorrow, a completely different proposition, Dr. Bagaric, and it's this: that the HVO brought about the conditions in East Mostar and they saw to it that those conditions remained appalling for month after month. That's the case that I'm going to put to you. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand, but I don't accept. I don't think that is the truth, at least not the entire truth. The whole truth would be that before the conflict in Mostar, there had been a conflict in the valley of the Neretva River, in Konjic, where Bosniak Muslims had really committed a horrendous crime, not only in Grabovica but in that entire area, and step by step they were advancing toward Mostar. Therefore, if it had transpired, and I'm speaking as someone who was there all that time and who never knew whether they would live to see the next day, if the Muslim forces had been a little stronger, they would have taken Mostar and continued on to Capljina, because their politicians were not even ashamed to say it openly. So the whole situation was caused by that conflict, which was pure war. If there had been no resistance from the Croatian side, from the Croat side, then this would have happened entirely differently. And I'm sorry that these things happened at all, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I'm mindful of the time, because I absolutely want your evidence to be over by tomorrow, but there is something important on which I need to respond. You say that if the Muslims had taken Mostar, they could have gone on until Capljina, and you said that this didn't happen on account of the resistance. Does that mean that had there not been a resistance from the Croats, the Muslims would have taken Mostar and would have taken control over the whole territory?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm convinced of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll look into military aspects with General Praljak when he testifies. I'll come back to that matter then. Prosecutor, you can go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: I want to look with you, please, at the blockade of East Mostar, as I'm going to call it, and at the difficulties that there were in getting aid and supplies into East Mostar. All right? That's the topic, and I'm going to start, please, by looking at two documents from the Defence binder that you were provided with on Monday, the larger binder, and we're going to look just a little bit at the position in West Mostar. We start with 2D00714, please, 2D00714. And, Dr. Bagaric, can you help us, please. Towards the end of the first paragraph on the first page, we have a sentence which reads: "During the previous week, the Central Medicines Depot received four valuable shipments of humanitarian aid ..." Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Page 1? 2D714, on page 1?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Page 1. And if you look in the B/C/S, 11 or so lines down from the top, you can see on the left-hand margin there's the number "20.000." Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I can see it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: So during the previous week, the Central Medicines Depot, this is of the hospital on the west bank, received four valuable shipments of humanitarian aid, totalling around 20.000 Deutschemarks in value; yes?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's written there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Immediately before that is: "The supply of medicines and medical supplies at the HVO RB Mostar is satisfactory." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Next sentence?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: The sentence immediately before: "The supply of medicines and medical supplies ... is satisfactory." All right, so that's --

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: That's the week 7th to 13th September. If you turn on, please, to 2D00738, that's a document in which you're reporting to Bruno Stojic for the week August 3rd to August 10th, and again medical materials and medicines supply for the war hospital HVO Mostar is satisfactory. And then in the past week, the Central Drugs Warehouse of the Main Medical HQ, Croatian Community HB, accepted eight valuable drug shipments from donations worth around 500.000 Deutschemarks?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: And the position so far, as access to Mostar for supplies coming to the hospital on the west bank, was that if people wanted to send assistance to you, they could?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, but at this point I have to tell the Court what the truth is about this 500.000 Deutschemark. After the war, I was president of the board of the hospital in Mostar. These 500.000 Deutschemark -- this was written by those who sent us the medication, but out of those 500.000, we actually had some losses to dispose of that rubbish. I don't know the exact figure, but I know that the hospital spent a lot of money, and I'm not making this up. It was in the newspapers at the time. This was medication whose shelf life had expired. A truck comes from Germany, from a donor, and they drop it there. And you even have to say, Thank you. But we still had stocks of that after the war, and it cost us a lot to take it to waste disposal facilities in various places. But the Prosecutor is right, we were in a much better situation as far as medical supplies are concerned than the other side in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: But those shipments had no difficulty getting through to you, did they?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were unusable, most of them. The overwhelming majority of these medicines were unusable, but of course we received shipments of medication.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: You were in, as you say, a much better position on the west bank than was the case on the east bank?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Is the reason for that that the HVO controlled access to Mostar?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the better question would be: Was this caused by the war? And the answer is yes, the war is the real reason. In the circumstances, the west side of Mostar had a hinterland, a large area in depth shielded from the war, whereas the east side had a front-line running through it, and of course under those circumstances it was difficult to get through to the east side of Mostar. That's common knowledge. And it didn't depend only on HVO, whether something is able to get through or not; it also depended on the other side. That's where the front-line was.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: The HVO could agree for a convoy of humanitarian aid to come through its territory and to the east bank or it could withhold that agreement; is that not the case, Dr. Bagaric?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. It's a very tricky question, so I can't answer with a yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Well, have a look with me, please, at P04527 [Realtime transcript read in error "P024527"], it's in the same binder that you're -- no, sorry. It's in the smaller binder that you had today, the Prosecution's binder, P04527 [Realtime transcript read in error "P024527"].

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: And what we can see there is a document dated the 26th of August of 1993, and it's headed "Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, Defence Department, Military Police Administration, Mostar." Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: And the order is to this effect: "On all border crossings and in the entire territory controlled by the 5th Military Police Battalion, ensure a free passage, freedom of movement for personnel carriers, foreign journalists, humanitarian organisations' officials, and all other citizens who possess movement clearances signed by the following individuals." Then we have a list of names. Bruno Stojic is somebody who can grant one of those permits, Slobodan Bozic, from whom we've heard, Ivo Lucic, Mr. Praljak, Mr. Petkovic, Mr. Tole, and then at number 9, you?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's me, my name.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: And that's definitely you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Sorry, because I'm so meticulous sometimes. Page 89, line 12 and 13, two times a wrong number appears for the document. The "2" must be omitted. It is P04527.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Yes, it is. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Dr. Bagaric, you were one of those who could give authorisation for humanitarian organisations' officials to pass through the territory of Herceg-Bosna, according to this order; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not right. Your Honours, this -- first of all, I have never seen this document before, but it doesn't matter. I was certainly one of the people -- I was the person who led the Health Sector. I frequently begged people for this or that. What does this mean? Physicians come from various places and want to pass through to the hospital, and of course since it was a war zone, people's documents were checked and their movements were checked. I was personally the one who frequently asked for such approvals, and people naturally thought that I could provide certain signatures for our medical needs. But if you look at this carefully, it says "at all border crossings." They were not towards the East Mostar, they were towards the Republic of Croatia. It was needed for rotation of medical teams, transfers of our patients to other hospitals. What I said about this Ms. Sally Baker, whoever addressed me and I was able to help, I always helped, but those were individual requests and they were not frequent, because it made no sense to ask a doctor for that. So that was primarily for the purpose of ensuring or providing medical assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: When the HVO wanted to deny access for humanitarian aid, it was very straightforward. They simply didn't grant a permit. That's the position, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think it was exactly that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I see the time. I'm going to develop this tomorrow, but that might be an appropriate moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In terms of time, you have another hour and 40 minutes, approximately. The Registrar is going to calculate this, Prosecution. Witness, I have noticed that your answers are very long. Tomorrow, since we're all concerned with time, I'll ask you to be shorter in your answers and try and avoid political reasonings. I know that you're a politician and that you're a good speaker, but please be extremely concise so that the Prosecution can ask a question and have a specific answer, so that he can move on to something else quickly. So please make an effort. But I'm sure you will manage. I'll give the floor to my colleague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I apologise to the parties for being absent tomorrow due to an academic engagement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There will be no extra time. Your evidence will finish tomorrow. The Prosecution will have an hour and 45 minutes. I hope that he will endeavour to reduce time. I'm sure that the Stojic Defence has additional questions, redirect questions, but I hope that this will take place very quickly. So I wish you all a pleasant evening, and I'll see you all tomorrow at 2.15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
